fragments.note: Hymn/Ode to Aphrodite — the only poem of Sappho's transmitted essentially complete; preserved by quotation in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, On Literary Composition.
Invocation of Aphrodite to a garden sanctuary; uniquely preserved on a potsherd (ostracon) rather than papyrus.
Prayer for the safe seafaring return of her brother Charaxos; part of the 'Brothers' cycle, on papyrus.
Further prayer concerning Charaxos, touching on his entanglement with a Naucratis courtesan; continues the Brothers material on a damaged papyrus.
Priamel on what is most beautiful on earth, illustrated by Helen's departure for Troy; addressed with reference to Anactoria. Same numbering in Lobel-Page.

Cult hymn to Hera (with Zeus and Dionysus) tied to the Lesbian sanctuary of Messon, invoking the Atreidae's prayer before Troy; text substantially extended beyond the older Lobel-Page version by the Green Collection papyrus (P.GC inv. 105).
Address urging the singer Abanthis to perform a song about Gongyla; two joined fragmentary stanzas on one papyrus.
Wedding-occasion fragment addressed to a girl nearing marriage, with imperative summons to companions and nightingale imagery.
The 'he seems to me equal to the gods' poem — first-person catalog of physical symptoms on watching a beloved woman with a man; quoted whole by [Longinus], On the Sublime.
Simile of stars around the moon, transmitted via Eustathius; often discussed alongside fr. 96.
Narrative epithalamian account of the wedding of Hector and Andromache at Troy, unusual among Sappho's fragments for its epic/narrative mode; papyrus (P.Oxy. 1232 + 2076).
Simile comparing the onset of Eros to a wind striking mountain oaks.
Fragment on a lover's arrival and the quieting of longing.
Two-line couplet recalling a past love for a girl named Atthis.
Polemic addressed to an uncultivated woman, warning of oblivion after death; transmitted by Stobaeus.

The 'Tithonus poem,' on old age and the myth of Tithonus and Dawn; the older Lobel-Page text (from Athenaeus, lines 11-22) substantially completed by the 2004 Cologne papyrus, a landmark modern discovery.
Fragmentary invocation of the god of Dreams together with night and Aphrodite.
Farewell scene recalling shared pleasures with a departing companion — garlands, perfumes, choral dancing; Berlin papyrus.
Expression of a longing for death, mentioning Gongyla and Hermes' role guiding souls to the underworld; fragmentary papyrus.
Consolation concerning a woman now among Lydian women, likened to the moon outshining the stars; addressee sometimes identified as Arignota; papyrus.
Paired fragments on hairbands/headdresses across three generations of women (Sappho's mother, Sappho, her daughter Cleis), set against a backdrop of political exile.
Short dialogue-style complaint to her mother about being unable to weave, overcome by desire for a boy through Aphrodite's agency.
Address to Hesperus, the evening star.
Simile of an unreachable apple ripening on the highest bough, cited by ancient critics as bridal imagery.
Simile of a hyacinth trampled underfoot by shepherds in the mountains; also numbered 105(c) in Lobel-Page.
Wedding hymn calling on carpenters to raise the roof-beam, comparing the bridegroom to Ares.
Wedding hymn praising the bridegroom's good fortune and the bride's grace.
Dialogue between the bride and personified Virginity at the moment of its departure.
Definition of Eros as bittersweet and limb-loosening; address to Atthis.
Short poem on her daughter Cleis, likened to a golden flower.

The 'moon has set' / Midnight-poem quatrain; preserved without attribution in Hephaestion's metrical handbook, so Sapphic authorship is disputed among editors (= Page, PMG adesp. 976); included in Voigt's corpus.

fragments.id: Brothers Poem (P.Sapph.Obbink, no traditional Voigt no.)
fragments.note: Previously unknown poem on anxiety over Charaxos' seafaring and hope for the maturation of brother Larichos; published 2014 from the Obbink papyrus; overlaps thematically with Voigt/Lobel-Page frr. 5, 9, 15-18.

Newly recovered continuation/correction of fr. 26 Voigt from the same 2014 papyrus, addressing Kypris/Aphrodite on recurring erotic suffering; substantially revises the sense of the previously known fragmentary lines.

sourced.variants:
All three fetched print recensions (Perseus/Radermacher; Wharton 1885; Cox 1924) transmit the SAME ancient witness — the quotation embedded in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, De Compositione Verborum 23 — so differences between them reflect (a) the real instability of Dionysius's own medieval manuscript tradition (sigla P, F, M, V etc., which disagree at several points) as resolved differently by each editor, and, in the two archive.org OCR scans, (b) some probable scanning noise. Line-by-line comparison against the Perseus/Radermacher text given above:

Line 1: Wharton and Cox both print "ἀθάνατ᾽" (agreeing with Perseus); a separate manuscript variant reported for this line in Dionysius's tradition (per the critical apparatus in J. M. Edmonds's 1922 Loeb, consulted but too OCR-corrupted to quote verbatim) is the poem's very first word: "ποικιλόθρον᾽" (richly-/rainbow-throned) is the majority reading, but some manuscripts of Dionysius read "ποικιλόφρον᾽" (many-wiled/subtle-minded) instead — a variant explicitly noted by Wharton too ("ποικιλόθρον᾽... is by some read ποικιλόφρον᾽").

Line 3: Perseus/Cox read "μηδ᾽ ὀνίαισι"; Wharton reads "μήτ᾽ ὀνίαισι" (μηδ᾽/μήτ᾽ — a genuine correlative-particle variant, not OCR noise, since both letter-sequences are equally legible).

Line 5: Perseus "τύδ᾽... αἴ ποκα"; Wharton/Cox "τυίδ᾽... αἴποτα/αἴποτὰ" — spelling/word-division variants for the same adverbs ("hither"; "if ever").

Line 9: Perseus reads the Aeolic-dialect form "ὐπασδεύξαισα" (from *ζεύγνυμι with the Aeolic -σδ- reflex); both Wharton and Cox instead print the Atticized "ὑποζεύξαισα" — a well-known crux in Sappho scholarship, since ὐπασδεύξαισα is the harder, more distinctively Aeolic reading.

Line 11: Perseus prints the crasis form "ὠράνᾤθερος" (ὠράνω + αἴθερος run together with a coronis); Wharton and Cox instead print the two words uncrased, "ὠράνω αἴθε-ρος/-ρας" (Wharton has "-ρας", Cox has "-ρος"). Perseus/Cox read "διὰ μέσσω"; Wharton reads "διὰ μίσσω" (μέσσω is the standard Doric/Aeolic form for "middle"; μίσσω is almost certainly a Wharton-scan OCR misreading of epsilon as iota rather than a real variant). Perseus reads "διννῆντες"; Wharton/Cox read "δινεῦντες" (a real orthographic variant of the participle "whirring/whirling").

Line 13: Cox reads "τὺ δ᾽" as "σὺ δ᾽" — a real pronoun variant (Aeolic τύ vs. the more familiar σύ) also visible against Perseus's "τὺ δ᾽".

Line 14: Perseus reads "ὄττι δἦν τὸ πέπονθα"; Wharton/Cox instead read "ὅττι/ὄττι δηὖτε πέπονθα" — a substantive variant (δἦν τὸ vs. δηὖτε) affecting the sense of "what I have suffered [again]".

Line 16: Perseus reads "κὤττ᾽ ἔμω μάλιστα"; Wharton/Cox read "κὤττι μοι μάλιστα" — pronoun-form variant (ἔμω vs. μοι).

Line 17: Perseus/Cox read "τίνα δηὖτε πείθω" (πείθω as the finite verb "I persuade"); Wharton instead capitalizes and prints "τίνα δεῦτε Πείθω" (treating Peitho, "Persuasion", as a personified goddess-figure) — an interpretive/textual variant with real consequences for how the line is construed, reflecting older (Bergk-era) editorial practice.

Line 26: Perseus reads "ἰμάρρει"; Wharton reads "ἱμέρρει"; Cox reads "ἰμμέρρει" — three different spellings of the same Aeolic verb-form ("[my heart] yearns/desires"), illustrating ongoing uncertainty in the manuscript/editorial tradition about this word's exact orthography.

A further crux reported in the Edmonds 1922 Loeb apparatus (not independently re-verified against a clean digital source because that scan's Greek OCR was too corrupted to quote reliably) concerns line 10: the transmitted manuscript reading "περὶ γᾶς μελαίνας" (which both Perseus and Wharton/Cox print, as above) was emended by some 20th-century editors to "πότι/προτὶ γᾶν μέλαιναν" on grounds of Homeric idiom; this is a conjectural EMENDATION rather than an attested manuscript variant, and is not reflected in any of the three texts actually quoted above.

No comparison against the papyrus (P.Oxy. 2288) or against Hephaestion's quotation could be made, since no verbatim text for either was recoverable from a fetched source in this session (see the caveats and the corresponding witness notes above).
sourced.caveats:
1) The Greek text given is verbatim from a page actually fetched (raw HTML of the Perseus Digital Library reader for Dionysius of Halicarnassus, De Compositione Verborum 23, urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0081.tlg012, ed. Radermacher), cross-checked against two other independently fetched public-domain print editions of the same quotation (Wharton 1885 and Cox 1924, both via archive.org/Wikisource). All three agree closely, so I am confident this represents the genuine transmitted text of Dionysius's quotation, essentially the whole poem (7 Sapphic stanzas, 28 verses) — matching the framing that this is Sappho's only poem transmitted essentially complete.

2) P.Oxy. XXI 2288 (2nd c. CE), the sole papyrus witness to this poem, is real and is cataloged (DCLP/TM/LDAB 62698) — I fetched that catalog record directly — but its actual transcribed letters are NOT available on papyri.info/DCLP (the edition field is empty there) nor could I reach the 1951 P.Oxy. XXI print edition or the 2024 ZPE re-edition online. I have therefore NOT included any papyrus reading and have NOT claimed the papyrus agrees or disagrees with the Dionysius text at any point — that comparison remains unverified and would require access to the print/PDF edition, which was outside what I could fetch in this session.

3) Hephaestion's Enchiridion is widely cited in the secondary literature (Wharton's note; Edmonds's Loeb apparatus) as quoting at least the opening stanza as a metrical example, but I could not locate a fetchable page giving that quotation's actual Greek wording, so it is listed as an attested-but-unverified witness only, with no text attributed to it.

4) J. M. Edmonds's 1922 Loeb 'Lyra Graeca' (archive.org lyragraecavolume00edmo_534), though genuinely public-domain and genuinely fetched, has Greek-text OCR so corrupted (systematic substitution of look-alike Latin letters for Greek ones, e.g. 'TioiKL\\69 pov' for 'Ποικιλόθρον') that I judged it unsafe to quote as "verbatim" Greek; I only paraphrased two apparatus-note variants from it (the ποικιλόθρον᾽/ποικιλόφρον᾽ alternative and the γᾶς/γᾶν crux) rather than presenting corrupted OCR as if it were the primary text.

5) Per the task's absolute rule, no English (or any modern-language) translation is included anywhere above; where fetched pages carried facing English translations (Wharton, Cox/Wikisource), that English was read only to help locate section boundaries and was then discarded — only the Greek spans were extracted into this output.

witnesses.source: Ostracon Florentinum (PSI XIII 1300) — a potsherd, 3rd–2nd c. BC, from Egypt
witnesses.edition: Editio princeps: M. Norsa, Annali della R. Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa, ser. II vol. 6 (1937), pp. 8ff.; transcription consulted as reproduced by 'The Digital Sappho' project (fragment page), which cites the Norsa edition directly beneath the text.
witnesses.note: The only witness that preserves the poem continuously, across four stanzas (16 lines). Several words are damaged or lost, marked with square brackets in the transcription (e.g. ἐπ[ὶ τόνδ]ε, ὄππ[ᾳ τοι], μαλί[αν], [λι]βανώντῳ); lines 11–12 are almost entirely lost, shown as bare '[' in the transcription consulted. This is the text given in greek_text above.

witnesses.source: Hermogenes of Tarsus, Περὶ ἰδεῶν λόγου (On Types of Style), late 2nd c. AD
witnesses.edition: Greek text as printed by Edwin Marion Cox, The Poems of Sappho (London, 1924), numbered there as the independent 'Fragment 5' (this book predates the 1937 ostracon publication, so Cox did not yet know it belonged to the same poem).
witnesses.note: Quotes only the couplet corresponding to the ostracon's stanza 2 (≈lines 5–8). Greek as transcribed on that page: 'ἀμφὶ δ᾽ ὔδωρ / ψῦχρον ὤνεμος κελάδει δἰ ὔσδων / μαλίνων, αἰθυσσομέμων δὲ φύλλων / κῶμα κατάρρει.' Cox's accompanying note records that Demetrius, Περὶ ἑρμηνείας (On Style), c. 150 AD, also refers to this same passage as part of 'Sappho's description of the garden of the nymphs' — a testimonium naming the passage rather than an independent quotation of its wording.

witnesses.source: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, Book 11 (traditionally cited at Kaibel/Casaubon ~463e)
witnesses.edition: G. Kaibel, Athenaei Naucratitae Dipnosophistarum libri XV (Teubner) — manuscript-based critical text, consulted via the 'Digital Athenaeus' Kaibel-text search tool
witnesses.note: Quotes only the equivalent of the ostracon's stanza 4 (≈lines 13–16), recast to fit Athenaeus's own sentence. Greek as returned from the Kaibel text search: 'ἐλθέ, Κύπρι, χρυσίαισιν ἐν κυλίκεσσιν ἁβρῶς συμμεμιγμένον θαλίαισι νέκταρ οἰνοχοοῦσα.'

witnesses.source: Same Athenaeus quotation (Deipnosophistae 11), in a second edition for comparison
witnesses.edition: Edwin Marion Cox, The Poems of Sappho (London, 1924), numbered there as the independent 'Fragment 6'
witnesses.note: Cox prints an Aeolicizing restoration of the same Athenaeus passage rather than the raw manuscript spelling: 'Ἔλθε, Κύπρι, / χρυσίαισιν ἐν κυλίκεσσιν ἄβραις / συμμεμιγμένον θαλίαισι νέκταρ / οἰνοχόεισα.' Compare against witness 3 above (ἄβραις/ἁβρῶς, οἰνοχόεισα/οἰνοχοοῦσα) — an editorial-restoration variant, not a manuscript variant.

sourced.variants:
Stanza 2 (ostracon lines 5–8) vs. Hermogenes' quotation:
- Ostracon: ἐν δ' ὔδωρ ψῦχρον κελάδει δι' ὔσδων μαλίνων, βρόδοισι δὲ παῖς ὀ χῶρος ἐσκίαστ', αἰθυσσομένων δὲ φύλλων κῶμα κατέρρει.
- Hermogenes (per Cox 1924 transcription): ἀμφὶ δ᾽ ὔδωρ ψῦχρον ὤνεμος κελάδει δἰ ὔσδων μαλίνων, αἰθυσσομέμων δὲ φύλλων κῶμα κατάρρει.
- Differences: (1) ἐν δ' (ostracon, "and in it...") vs ἀμφὶ δ' (Hermogenes, "and round about..."); (2) Hermogenes' text supplies an explicit subject ὤνεμος ("the wind") for κελάδει, absent from the ostracon, where the water itself is the subject; (3) Hermogenes' quotation entirely omits the ostracon's clause "βρόδοισι δὲ παῖς ὀ χῶρος ἐσκίαστ'" (roses shading the ground), passing directly from μαλίνων to αἰθυσσομέμων — i.e. Hermogenes quotes a shorter, non-continuous excerpt, not a variant reading of the full stanza; (4) κατέρρει (ostracon) vs κατάρρει (Hermogenes as printed by Cox) — likely an orthographic/accentual difference rather than a substantive one.

Stanza 4 (ostracon lines 13–16) vs. Athenaeus's quotation:
- Ostracon: ἔνθα δὴ σύ . . . . ἔλοισα Κύπρι χρυσίαισιν ἐν κυλίκεσσιν ἄβρως ὀμμεμείχμενον θαλίαισι νέκταρ οἰνοχόαισον.
- Athenaeus, Kaibel ms. text: ἐλθέ, Κύπρι, χρυσίαισιν ἐν κυλίκεσσιν ἁβρῶς συμμεμιγμένον θαλίαισι νέκταρ οἰνοχοοῦσα.
- Differences: (1) Athenaeus's quotation opens with the plain imperative ἐλθέ, Κύπρι ("[Come], Cypris"), replacing the ostracon's ἔνθα δὴ σύ . . . . ἔλοισα Κύπρι construction (a participial clause built around "you, having taken..."); (2) ὀμμεμείχμενον (ostracon, Aeolic-dialect perfect passive participle) vs συμμεμιγμένον (Athenaeus, Attic/koine-dialect form of the same participle) — a genuine dialectal substitution; (3) οἰνοχόαισον (ostracon, 2nd-person imperative "pour!") vs οἰνοχοοῦσα (Athenaeus, feminine nominative present participle "pouring"), each grammatically fitted to its own sentence frame; (4) ἄβρως/ἁβρῶς is the same adverb differing only in breathing/accent as printed in the two sources consulted.
- Additionally, the two modern print sources consulted for the Athenaeus quotation itself disagree editorially: Kaibel's manuscript-based text (ἁβρῶς, οἰνοχοοῦσα) vs Cox's 1924 Aeolic-restored text (ἄβραις, οἰνοχόεισα) — see witnesses 3–4.
sourced.caveats: (1) The ostracon transcription was obtained from a single fetched secondary transcription (The Digital Sappho project page), which itself cites Norsa's 1937 editio princeps; I was not able to independently cross-check it against a second full transcription of the ostracon (e.g. Lobel-Page or Voigt's apparatus, or a facsimile), because the site I tried for that purpose (inamidst.com/stuff/sappho) returned repeated HTTP 503 errors and could not be fetched, and Wikipedia's 'Sappho 2' article (checked twice, including a request for its raw wikitext) discusses the fragment at length but does not itself reproduce the Greek text at all. (2) Lines 11–12 of the ostracon are badly damaged; the source consulted here shows them only as an open bracket '[' with no further legible letters given, so I have reproduced exactly that rather than supplying letters from memory. (3) Edmonds/Cox's 1924 edition predates the 1937 publication of the ostracon, so it treats the Hermogenes- and Athenaeus-preserved excerpts as two separate, independent 'fragments' (his nos. 5 and 6); I have matched them to the corresponding stanzas of the later, unified ostracon text based on content. (4) A third fragment adjacent in Cox's numbering ('Fragment 7', quoting Strabo: Ἤ σε Κύπρος καὶ Πάφος ἢ Πάνορμος) is NOT part of this poem — a search confirmed it is catalogued as a separate Sappho fragment (Digital Sappho's fr. 35) — and has accordingly been excluded from the witness list here despite its topical/thematic proximity (also an Aphrodite-invocation) in the older edition. (5) No modern-language translation of any of the Greek quoted above is included anywhere in this output, per the task's absolute rule.
sourced.note: Invocation of Aphrodite to a garden sanctuary; uniquely preserved on a potsherd (ostracon) rather than papyrus.

sourced.variants:
Because fr. 5 survives on only ONE physical ancient witness (P.Oxy. 7, a single lacunose papyrus sheet — no ancient author is known to quote its verses; Herodotus 2.134–135 and Athenaeus 13.596b–d tell the Charaxos/Rhodopis-Doricha story in prose but do not cite Sappho's actual words from this poem), the "variants" here are between modern editors' restorations of the same damaged papyrus, not between independent ancient copies. Three recensions were fetched and compared:

1. BLASS 1898 (in Grenfell & Hunt, editio princeps) — reconstructs the opening as an appeal to the Nereids alone, with Aphrodite addressed only indirectly via the vocative ἄμβροτε in line 5: "[σὺν δὲ καὶ ὔμμες], ὦ φίλα]ι Νηρήϊδες, ἀβλάβη[ν ..." Blass believed one full stanza was lost before the preserved text and that the poem might end at line 20. His notes flag στ. 4 (lines 13–16) as much less certain than stt. 1–3, and lines 17–20 as beyond confident restoration (only a skeletal "σὺ [δὲ] λύγ[ρ᾽ ἐρέμ]να / νύκτι πάντα κατ]θεμ[έν]α κάκαν" ventured for line 18–19).

2. EDMONDS 1922 (Lyra Graeca I, Loeb, no. "86"/36 "εἰς Νηρηΐδας," citing "Ox. Pap. 7," with apparatus crediting restorations to "Blass, Buecheler, B[ell], and Z[ ]"; text fetched from the archive.org OCR of this edition) diverges from Blass at several points, e.g. line 3 "[κώ]σσα ᾧ θύμῳ κε θέλῃ γένεσθαι" (dative pronoun form differs from Blass's "Ϝ[ῷ]"); line 7 "κώνίαν ἔ]χθροισι" vs Blass's "κ]ών[αν ἔ]χθροισι"; and especially lines 14–16, where Edmonds prints "[χέρρεν, ἀλ]λ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀγ[λαΐ]ᾳ πολίταν / [ἀββάλην ἄλλως, [ὄτα] νῆ κε δαῦτ᾽ οὐ[δὲν διὰ μά]κρω" — a substantially different restoration of the syntax from Blass's "κέρρον ἦλλ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀγλαΐ]α πολίταν, / καὶ βράχυ ζ]αλεῖπ[ον ἀ]νῆκε δαὺτ᾽ οὔ / κεν διὰ μά]κρω." Edmonds also adds a further stanza-fragment restoration for lines 17–20 not attempted by Blass: "[καὶ συνάορ]ον, αἴ κ[ε θέλη, ἀξίοι]σιν ... [ἐν λέχεσσ᾽ Ἴδην· σὺ [δέ], κύν[ ᾽Ερέμ]να, / [ῥῖνα πρὸς γᾶι] θεμ[έν]α κακάν[ ]." His footnote apparatus records that these last supplements are "restored by Blass, Diels, Jurenka, Smyth, Wil[amowitz], Z[ ]."

3. CAMPBELL 1982 (Greek Lyric I, Loeb; text as reproduced on The Digital Sappho, https://digitalsappho.org/fragments/fr5/), representing the Lobel–Page/Voigt-era text that incorporates the supplementary papyrus scrap P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 6 (unknown to Blass and Edmonds, since P.Oxy. 2289 was only published by Lobel in 1951): "[Κύπρι καὶ] Νηρήιδες ἀβλάβη[ν μοι / τὸν κασί]γνητον δ[ό]τε τυίδ᾽ ἴκεσθα[ι / κὤσσα ϝ]οι θύμῳ κε θέλῃ γένεσθαι / πάντα τε]λέσθην, / ὄσσα δὲ πρ]όσθ᾽ ἄμβροτε πάντα λῦσα[ι / καὶ φίλοισ]ι ϝοῖσι χάραν γένεσθαι / κὠνίαν ἔ]χθροισι, γένοιτο δ᾽ ἄμμι / πῆμ᾽ ἔτι μ]ηδ᾽ εἴς· / τὰν κασιγ]νήταν δὲ θέλοι πόησθαι / ἔμμορον] τίμας [ὀν]ίαν δὲ λύγραν / ]οτοισι π[ά]ροιθ᾽ ἀχεύων / ].να / ].εισαΐω[ν] τὸ κέγχρω / ]λ᾽ επαγ[ορί]ᾳ πολίταν / ]λλως[...]νηκε δ᾽ αῦτ᾽ οὐ / ]κρω[ / ]οναικ[ ]εο[ ].ι / ]..[.]ν· σὺ [δ]ὲ Κύπ[ρ]ι σ[έμ]να / ]θεμ[έν]α κάκαν [ / ]ι." Two significant divergences from Blass: (a) line 1 is restored with Κύπρι named directly ("[Κύπρι καὶ] Νηρήιδες") rather than Blass's "[σὺν δὲ καὶ ὔμμες], ὦ φίλα]ι Νηρήϊδες..."; (b) line 18, where Blass reads "σὺ [δὲ] λύγ[ρ᾽ ἐρέμ]να," Campbell's text reads "σὺ [δ]ὲ Κύπ[ρ]ι σ[έμ]να" — i.e. Aphrodite/Κύπρις is named again near the poem's end rather than Blass's "grievous darkness" phrase — a divergence driven by the added readings from P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 6.

No variant is a genuine "manuscript" variant (different ancient wording); all three are competing modern conjectural completions of the same lacunae in the one surviving papyrus, and the underlying legible papyrus letters (the diplomatic transcription given above) are consistent across all consultations of P.Oxy. 7.

sourced.caveats:
(1) This fragment survives on only a single ancient physical witness, the papyrus P.Oxy. 7 (extended in modern scholarship by the small joining fragment P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 6). No ancient author is known to quote Sappho fr. 5's actual wording as a testimonium; my search confirmed that Herodotus (2.134–135) and Athenaeus (13.596b–d), who do discuss the Charaxos/Rhodopis-Doricha episode that this poem concerns, narrate it in prose and do not cite these verses — they are more often associated with fr. 15. So "witnesses" here means competing modern papyrological/editorial recensions of one damaged papyrus, not independent ancient copies, per the task's own allowance for "two independent papyri" not being available in this case.
(2) Roughly 80% of the running text is editorial conjecture in brackets; only the diplomatic, unrestored letter-sequence (given first, in majuscule) is directly "primary ancient text" in the strictest sense — the three restorations quoted (Blass 1898, Edmonds 1922, Campbell 1982/Lobel-Page-Voigt) are scholarly reconstructions of varying vintage and confidence, explicitly presented as such by their editors.
(3) OCR quality of both archive.org full-text scans (1898 Oxyrhynchus Papyri I and 1922 Lyra Graeca I) is poor in places (stray characters, misread diacritics, occasional dropped/duplicated letters), a known limitation of that automated transcription layer rather than of the printed editions themselves; where possible I cross-checked readings against a second fetched source (the Latinum Substack close paraphrase of G&H 1898 pp. 11–12, and the Digital Sappho reproduction of Campbell 1982) to reduce the risk of reporting OCR corruption as genuine text. Residual uncertainty in a handful of individual letters/accents in the Edmonds 1922 quotation should be assumed.
(4) I was not able to obtain a scan of P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 6 itself (the 1951 Lobel edition, P.Oxy. vol. XXI) directly; the Oxford Sackler Digital Sappho image-portal page for it returned HTTP 403 and could not be fetched, so its contribution is reported only indirectly via the Campbell 1982 composite text.
(5) Per the task's absolute rule, no English (or Latin, which the Grenfell & Hunt source-material and the Substack secondary source both also supplied) translation has been included anywhere above; only Greek text, citations, and philological/codicological description of the witnesses appear.

sourced.variants:
Only one ancient source survives for this fragment (the single papyrus P.Oxy. 1231, fr. 1 col. I + fr. 3), so there is no independent second ancient copy — but the papyrus is so damaged that successive modern editors have restored/read the gaps differently, producing real, substantive variant texts of the same lacunae. Key crux, ll.9-10 (numbering as in the papyrus column):

(1) Grenfell & Hunt, editio princeps (P.Oxy. X, 1914): κα[ί σ]ε πι[κροτέρ]αν ἔπευρ[εν ('...found you more bitter' — comparative adjective, 3rd sg. AORIST INDICATIVE ἔπευρεν) ... [οἱ] δὲ καυχάσαντο τόδ᾽ ἐννέ[ποντες ('and THEY boasted, saying this' — 3rd pl. indicative, plural subject).

(2) Edmonds, Lyra Graeca (1922), fr.37: κα[ί σ]ε πι[κροτέρ]αν ἐπεύρ[οι (same comparative πικροτέραν as Grenfell & Hunt, but AORIST OPTATIVE ἐπεύροι, 'may she find you more bitter') ... [μη]δὲ καυχάσαιτο τόδ᾽ ἐννέ[ποισα ('nor may SHE boast, saying' — 3rd sg. optative + fem. sg. participle, singular subject) — a hybrid between the other two readings.

(3) Modern standard text (Campbell 1982 / Voigt-type, per Digital Sappho / Haverford): κα[ί σ]ε πι[κροτάτ]α̣ν ἐπεύρ[οι ('may she find you most bitter' — SUPERLATIVE πικροτάταν, not comparative, aorist optative ἐπεύροι) ... μη]δὲ καυχάσ[α]ιτο τόδ᾽ ἐννέ[ποισα (same as Edmonds' reading here).

So across the tradition there are three distinct restorations of the adjective (πικροτέραν 'more bitter' in 1914 and Edmonds 1922, vs. πικροτάταν 'most bitter' in the later standard text), two distinct restorations of the verb (indicative ἔπευρεν in 1914 vs. optative ἐπεύροι in Edmonds and the standard text), and two distinct restorations of the following clause's grammatical subject/number (plural indicative οἱ δὲ καυχάσαντο ... ἐννέποντες in 1914, i.e. unnamed people boasting, vs. singular optative μηδὲ καυχάσαιτο ... ἐννέποισα in Edmonds and the standard text, i.e. a prayer that Doricha herself NOT be able to boast). The 1914 princeps' ll.9-10 restorations are explicitly credited there to Wilamowitz-Moellendorff ('Restored by W-M'), and Doricha's name in l.11 is also credited to Wilamowitz-Moellendorff's recognition, cross-checked there against Posidippus' epigram on Doricha quoted from Athenaeus.

A further, smaller variant at l.5: Campbell/Digital-Sappho restores the line-end as ὄσσα δὲ πρ]όσθ᾽ [ἄμ]βροτε κῆ[να λῦσαι ('...to atone for/undo those things', infinitive), whereas the compilation site inamidst.com's presentation of the same lacuna gives [ὄσσα δὲ πρ]όσθ᾽[ ἄμ]βροτε κῆ[ν᾽ ἔλυσεν] ('...undid those things', 3rd sg. aorist indicative) — again a comparative/indicative-vs-infinitive style divergence in how editors have filled the same gap.

Orthographic/accentual micro-variants also appear between recensions of ll.11-12 (e.g. ὡς vs ὠς; [εἰς] bracketed identically in all).
sourced.caveats:
(1) This fragment survives on a SINGLE ancient physical witness — the papyrus roll P.Oxy. 1231 (2nd century AD), fr. 1 col. I (lines 1-12) supplemented by the separately-numbered fr. 3 of the same roll — first published by Grenfell & Hunt in 1914. There is no second independent ancient copy and no ancient author is known to quote this poem's actual wording verbatim (Herodotus, Strabo, Athenaeus and Posidippus all discuss Charaxos/Doricha/Rhodopis as historical/biographical background, and Posidippus' epigram — quoted above — references Sappho's fame for having sung of Doricha, but none of them quotes fr.15's Greek text itself). So 'multiple witnesses' here means multiple modern editorial RECENSIONS of one very damaged papyrus, not multiple ancient copies — I have reported these recensions and their variants as instructed, but flag that the manuscript tradition proper has only one leg.
(2) The papyrus is badly damaged: even in the best-preserved lines (9-12) roughly half the letters are editorial restoration inside square brackets; lines 1-8 are so fragmentary that even the 1914 editio princeps prints them only as a near-illegible diplomatic transcript, and the archive.org OCR of that specific diplomatic-transcript block (a scan of Plate II mixed with Latin/Greek OCR confusion) was too corrupted for me to responsibly quote letter-by-letter as 'verbatim' — I have therefore given lines 1-8 only in the two later, cleanly re-edited recensions (Campbell/Digital-Sappho and, partially, inamidst.com), and explicitly did not reconstruct the 1914 diplomatic text of those lines from the garbled OCR.
(3) 'Fragment 15' is Lobel-Page/Voigt numbering (also the numbering used by Campbell's Loeb and by Digital Sappho). Edmonds' 1922 Loeb numbers the same papyrus passage as his own fragment '37' (he predates and does not use Lobel-Page numbers). I identified this correspondence myself by matching the papyrus source citation (P.Oxy. 1231. 1. i, same lines) and the shared Doricha/Kypri wording — this cross-identification is my own inference from the fetched texts, not asserted by either source in those terms.
(4) One source I initially found via web search (a search-tool synthesis, not a page I fetched directly) claimed P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 11 independently corroborates the 'πικροτάταν' reading. On directly fetching and reading the raw HTML of that source myself, this was incorrect: P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 11, as presented there, is a separate, almost entirely illegible scrap that the page assigns to a DIFFERENT fragment (Lobel-Page 14), not to fragment 15; the 'πικροτάταν' line in that source is sourced only to P.Oxy. 1231, not to 2289. I am flagging this explicitly so the false lead is not repeated: P.Oxy. 2289 is NOT a confirmed second witness to fr.15 based on anything I was able to verify by direct fetch.
(5) The 'Italian Wikipedia' variant reported under witness 4 is a tertiary, non-scholarly source relayed only secondhand (via inamidst.com quoting it) — I was not able to fetch it.wikipedia.org directly to confirm it myself, so it is included only as a recorded variant of record, with the caveat that its ultimate editorial authority is unverified.
(6) No English (or other modern-language) translation of the fragment appears anywhere in this output; where fetched pages contained English translations alongside the Greek, those were read and discarded, never reproduced.

sourced.variants:
No ancient quoting-author (testimonium) is attested for fr. 16 in any source consulted — unlike frr. 1, 31, 44, etc., it survives solely on papyrus. The significant variants found are between the ORIGINAL 1914 editio princeps of P.Oxy. 1231 (Grenfell & Hunt) and the modern consensus text (Lobel-Page/Voigt), the latter informed by the subsequently-published overlapping papyri (P.Oxy. 2166(a), P.S.I. 123, and P.GC. inv. 105):

1) Line 8 (τὸν πανάριστον): Grenfell & Hunt 1914 conjectured “[κρίννεν ἄριστον]” (i.e. a different verb, ‘judged best’) in place of the now-standard “τὸν [πανάρ]ιστον”.

2) Lines 9–12: Grenfell & Hunt 1914 printed “[ὅς τὸ πᾶν] σέβας Τροίαις ὄλεσσ[ἕ]ν, / [οὐδὲ π]αῖδος οὐδὲ φ[ίλ]ων το[κ]ήων / [οὐδὲν] ἐμνάσθη, ἀ[λλὰ] παράγαγ᾽ αὔταν / [Κύπρις ἔραι]σαν” — i.e. Helen ‘lost all reverence for Troy’, with no mention of her sailing there. The modern text, confirmed once P.Oxy. 2166(a) fr. 2 was published (1951) and adopted by Lobel-Page/Voigt, instead reads “καλλ[ίποι]σ᾽ ἔβα ’ς Τροΐαν πλέοι[σα / κωὐδ[ὲ πα]ῖδος οὐδὲ φίλων το[κ]ήων / πά[μπαν] ἐμνάσθη, ἀλλα παράγάγ᾽ αὔταν / αὔτικ' ἴδοι]σαν” — i.e. Helen sails away, and it is Kypris who leads her astray on catching sight of her. This is the single largest divergence between the earliest published transcription and the received text.

3) Line 19 (ἢ τὰ Λύδων ἄρματα καὶ ...ὅπλοισι): Grenfell & Hunt 1914 read “ἄρματα κὰν ὄπλοισι(ν)”; the modern text reads “ἄρματα καὶ πανόπλοις”.

4) Line 20 (final word): Grenfell & Hunt 1914 restored “[ἱππομ]άχεντας” (‘fighting on horseback/in chariots’); the modern text (Lobel-Page/Voigt) restores “πεσδομ]άχεντας” (‘fighting on foot’) — opposite sense for the restored participle.

5) Beyond line 20/24, modern editors differ among themselves (not an ancient-witness variant, but a live disagreement over how to fill the papyrus's lacunae in the Kypris stanza, ll. 13–16 Voigt, per the Eugesta article fetched at https://www.peren-revues.fr/eugesta/716): M. A. Santamaría Álvarez's text (based on Burris-Fish-Obbink 2014) differs from D. Obbink's own 'more conservative' text with full apparatus (in The Newest Sappho, 2016) at several points — e.g. Obbink prints only “[ · · ·άρ]ιῠτον” rather than committing to “[πανάρ]ιῠτον” at line 8; Obbink rejects M. L. West's supplement “σώφρον᾽ ἔοι]σαν” at line 12 as inconsistent with the papyrus's surviving ink-traces; and Obbink defends “τῷ]με” at the start of line 15, following J. Lidov, against other proposals. None of these differences are reflected in the greek_text field above, which follows the standard Lobel-Page-based redaction as given by greek-language.gr.
sourced.caveats: (1) Fragment 16 is preserved only fragmentarily; every word/word-ending printed above outside the small stretches of continuously-legible papyrus is an editorial SUPPLEMENT filling a lacuna — conventionally marked with square brackets in scholarly editions, which I have preserved from the greek-language.gr transcription (https://www.greek-language.gr/digitalResources/ancient_greek/anthology/poetry/browse.html?text_id=283, fetched directly), itself explicitly labelled 'Lobel-Page 16.1-20'. A parallel fetch of https://digitalsappho.org/fragments/fr16/ returned a Voigt-based text agreeing with it essentially word-for-word for lines 1-11 (only orthographic/apostrophe differences), which cross-confirms the transcription; digitalsappho's page apparently truncated before displaying lines 12-20, so those lines rest on the greek-language.gr fetch alone among the two direct modern-edition fetches (they are, however, independently corroborated by the raw 1914 papyrus transcription for the Lydian-chariots line, see below). (2) I independently fetched and grep'd the actual 1914 editio princeps (Grenfell & Hunt, Oxyrhynchus Papyri X) via its archive.org OCR text (https://archive.org/download/oxyrhynchuspapyr10gren/oxyrhynchuspapyr10gren_djvu.txt) to obtain a primary-source check; the OCR is imperfect (Greek diacritics and underdotted/uncertain letters are frequently garbled or dropped by the scanner), so I have not used it as the base text, only to verify wording and to document the 1914 vs. modern variants listed above, which are visible even through the OCR noise. (3) I was not able to independently verify, from the sources actually fetched, the EXACT line-range that P.S.I. 123 overlaps within fr. 16 (see note on that witness) — Grenfell & Hunt's own 1914 discussion associates P.S.I. 123 chiefly with the neighbouring Hera poem (fr. 17) rather than fr. 16, while the Lobel-Page/Voigt apparatus (as reported secondhand by digitalsappho.org) cites 'P.S.I. 123.1-2' among the sigla for fr. 16; I was not able to fetch the actual P.S.I. 123 publication (Vitelli & Norsa 1913) or a full modern critical apparatus (e.g. Voigt 1971 or Campbell's Loeb) to resolve this. (4) I could not fetch a page giving the precise word(s) P.GC. inv. 105 (2014) actually newly contributes to fr. 16's text (only that it 'added a few words' and helped fix the poem's endpoint at line 20); a full apparatus for that papyrus's exact readings would require access to Burris/Fish/Obbink, ZPE 189 (2014) or The Newest Sappho (2016), which I could not fetch as usable text (the one PDF I tried, a related Dutch-journal supplement, returned undecipherable binary/OCR garbage). (5) Per the task's requirement, no English or other modern-language translation of the poem is included anywhere above; all notes are strictly bibliographic/papyrological description of Greek-language witnesses.
sourced.note: Priamel on what is most beautiful on earth, illustrated by Helen's departure for Troy; addressed with reference to Anactoria. Same numbering in Lobel-Page.

witnesses.source: P.GC. inv. 105, Fr. 2 col. ii (the 'Green Collection' papyrus, sometimes called P.Sapph.Green)
witnesses.edition: editio princeps: S. Burris, J. Fish, D. Obbink, "New Fragments of Book 1 of Sappho," Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und Epigraphik 189 (2014) 1–28, text of fr. 17 at pp. 19–20 (diplomatic text left column / articulated text right column), commentary pp. 4–5 and 19–22
witnesses.note: Papyrus roll of Sappho Book 1, written in a formal calligraphic hand datable (on palaeographic grounds) to the late 2nd–first half of 3rd century AD. In the Green Collection, Oklahoma City (also cited as P.Sapph.Obbink's companion roll). Fr. 2 col. ii preserves the right-hand portions of lines corresponding to Sa. fr. 17.1–20 that were previously missing or wholly conjectural, plus (immediately following) what appears to be the opening of the next poem in the roll (Sa. fr. 18). Its readings were combined by the editors with the pre-existing witnesses P.Oxy. 1231 and PSI 123, which supply the left-hand portions of the same lines.

sourced.variants:
Because fr. 17 survives only on papyrus (no ancient author is known to quote it as a literary testimonium), the "variants" here are of two kinds: (A) actual differences of letters/accentuation between the papyrus witnesses themselves, and (B) the very large difference between the pre-2014 conjectural reconstruction (Lobel–Page/Voigt, built almost entirely from meter and guesswork for the right-hand halves of lines) and the post-2014 reconstructions once P.GC. inv. 105 supplied real papyrus letters for those halves.

(A) Witness-level variants noted in Burris–Fish–Obbink, ZPE 189 (2014):
- Line 3 (17.3): PSI 123 reads ερτον (ἐρᾰτον) where P.Oxy. 1231 and P.GC. inv. 105 agree on ἀράταν — flagged by the editors as a metrically incorrect alternative in the PSI 123 tradition.
- Accentuation: of P.GC. inv. 105's seven clear accent marks, none coincides with an accent in the other witnesses at any point of overlap. P.GC. inv. 105 alone accents τόι at 17.4; P.Oxy. 1231 alone accents τύ at 17.7 and κάτ at 17.12 (both left unaccented, or the accent-bearing word differently divided, in P.GC. inv. 105).
- Line 6 (17.6): the exact spelling is debated — Burris–Fish–Obbink print πὲρ Εἴ[λιον] (a spelling paralleled in P.Ryl.Gr. 22), on the basis of the P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 9 traces, against Page's earlier Ἴλιον; Ferrari's 2014 edition instead prints πὲρ Εἴ[λειον].
- Line 12 (17.12): Burris–Fish–Obbink print κὰτ τὸ π[άλ][αον] (πάλαον, comparing the spelling παλάων at Alcaeus fr. 169a.5), while Ferrari's edition prints the more familiar κὰτ τὸ πάλ[αιον].
- Line 16 (17.16): Burris–Fish–Obbink leave μέτρ’ ὀλ[ open, tentatively suggesting the verb ὀλολύσδην (comparing Alcaeus fr. 130a.18–20 on the ritual ὀλολυγή of women at the same shrine); Ferrari's edition instead commits to the noun μέτρ' ὀλ̣[ολύγαϲ.
- Line 20 (17.20, final preserved word): Ferrari prints [Ἦ]ρ’ ἀπίκε[ϲθαι in full; Burris–Fish–Obbink leave the line-opening more open, ]ρ’ ἀπικε[.
- Crux at Ἀτρ[εϊδα]ι (line 3): the papyrus letters are compatible with either nominative plural Ἀτρέϊδαι ("the sons of Atreus," i.e. both Agamemnon and Menelaus) or dative singular Ἀτρεΐδᾳ ("for/to the son of Atreus," i.e. Menelaus alone); Burris–Fish–Obbink's commentary sets out both possibilities at length without deciding definitively, noting it bears on whether Sappho's version of the myth put one or both Atreidae on Lesbos.

(B) Recension-level variants — pre-2014 (Lobel–Page/Voigt, conjectural) vs. post-2014 (papyrus-based, Burris–Fish–Obbink / Ferrari) reconstructions of the same lines:
- Line 1: πλάσιον δή μ' [εὐχομέναι φανείη (old, wholly conjectural) vs. Πλάσιον δὴ µ[...]ω with the papyrus itself preserving only line-end traces (new; exact supplement still undetermined by the editors, who canvass μ[οι, a dative participle, or an imperative such as ἀ[γέσθ]ω/ἀ[είδ]ω without settling on one).
- Line 5: μ[άλα πόλλ' ἄεθλα (old conjecture, accusative) vs. μ[εγά]λοιϲ ἀέθλοιϲ (new papyrus reading, dative).
- Line 6: περ Ἴ̣[λιον ἔν τε πόντῳ (old conjecture, including "and on the sea") vs. πὲρ Εἴ[λιον/Εἴλειον]· ἄψερον δέ (new papyrus reading; πόντῳ has no basis in the papyrus and is replaced by ἄψερον δέ).
- Line 7: ὄδον περαίνην (old conjecture) vs. ὄ]δον γὰρ εὔρη[ν (new papyrus reading, with a γάρ-clause entirely unforeseen by earlier editors, per Burris–Fish–Obbink).
- Line 9: ἀντ[ίαον κάλεσσαι (old conjecture) vs. ἀντ[ίαον] πεδέλθην (new papyrus reading — a different verb, paralleled at Alcaeus fr. 129.19 in the same sanctuary context).
- Line 11: κ[ἄμοι πραϋμένης ἄρηξον (old conjecture, first-person singular personal request) vs. κ[αί ...] πόημεν (new papyrus reading, first-person plural — flagged by Burris–Fish–Obbink as the key new evidence that the poem is a choral cult-song, not the "personal" poem D. Page had inferred from the old, conjectural text).
- Line 13: ἄγνα καὶ κά̣[λα (old conjecture, "holy and beautiful[...]") vs. ἄγνα κ[αὶ κα]...ὄ]χλοϲ (new papyrus reading, continuing to a different word, ὄχλος).
- Lines 14–16: old text gives only isolated letters/line-fragments (π]αρθ[εν, ἀ]μφι.[, three wholly lost lines) where the new papyrus supplies continuous text: π]αρθέ[νων ... γ]υναίκων, ἀμφις[, μέτρ' ὀλ[ολύγας/ὀλολύσδην.
sourced.caveats:
All Greek text above was extracted verbatim from fetched sources, not reconstructed from memory: (1) the pre-2014 composite (Lobel–Page/Voigt) text from https://digitalsappho.org/fragments/fr17/ (WebFetch); (2) Ferrari's 2014 edition of the extended fragment, as quoted with citation in Jung Shaan Lee, "Why Hera? A comparative investigation into Sappho's Brothers poem and Fragment 17," Philomathes (University of Auckland, published in the APSU Philomathes journal), downloaded and read directly as a PDF from https://www.apsu.edu/philomathes/WhyHera.pdf; (3) the editio princeps diplomatic and articulated texts of P.GC. inv. 105 from Simon Burris, Jeffrey Fish, and Dirk Obbink, "New Fragments of Book 1 of Sappho," Zeitschrift für Papyrologie und Epigraphik 189 (2014) 1–28, downloaded and read directly as a PDF from https://newsappho.files.wordpress.com/2015/01/zpe-189-burris-fish-obbink.pdf.

Simplifications: the ZPE 189 diplomatic/articulated text in the original uses a multi-tier bracket system (plain letters = read in P.GC. 105 only; letters in upper half-brackets = read in P.GC. 105 and agreeing with another witness; letters in lower half-brackets = supplied from another witness where P.GC. 105 is not preserved; letters in square brackets = purely conjectural editorial supplement; underdots = uncertain individual letters) that cannot be fully reproduced in plain text; I have collapsed all of these into simple square brackets for restored/uncertain text, sacrificing some precision for readability. Readers who need the exact diplomatic distinctions should consult the cited ZPE 189 PDF directly (it also includes full palaeographical notes and an apparatus for every line).

No ancient author's quotation (testimonium) of fr. 17 is attested — unlike some other Sappho fragments, this poem is known only from papyrus copies of the Alexandrian book-edition, so all witnesses listed are papyrological. Line numbering (1–20) follows the conventional Voigt numbering used by all cited editions. The poem's text breaks off after line 20 in P.GC. inv. 105 into what the editors identify as the start of the following poem (Sa. fr. 18); I have flagged but not included that continuation as it does not belong to fr. 17 proper. I made every effort to exclude any English translation, paraphrase, or summary of Sappho's actual words from this output; all English text here concerns only sourcing, editions, papyrus dates/locations, and grammatical/textual facts about the witnesses.

sourced.variants:
Two recensions of the same single papyrus (P.Oxy. 1231) were located; no independent quoting-author testimonium (Athenaeus, Hephaestion, a lexicographer, etc.) for this poem turned up in searching.

(1) STRUCTURE. Voigt/Campbell (as on digitalsappho.org, reproduced in greek_text above) print one continuous 21-line composite poem formed by joining P.Oxy. 1231 fr. 12 (lines 1–8, very fragmentary) to fr. 15 (lines 9–21). Edmonds (1922), writing before Lobel's 1925 join, prints only the fr. 15 material as an independent short poem, his no. 45 'πρὸς Γόγγυλαν' — i.e. he has no counterpart at all to the fr. 12 stanza (]βλα.[ … ]δε).

(2) THE CRUX AT THE START OF THE SECOND (=EDMONDS') STANZA. Voigt/Campbell: "Γο]γγύλαν̣ [Ἄβ]α̣νθι λαβοισαν ἀ.[ / πᾶ[κτιν". Edmonds (OCR, verbatim as fetched): "[Γόγ]γυλα β[ρόδ]ανθι, λάβοισα Λύδα[ν]". The two editions construe the same papyrus letters differently: Voigt/Campbell take a vocative proper name Ἄβανθι as a second addressee (alongside Γόγγυλαν as accusative object), whereas Edmonds instead supplies a conjectural compound epithet βρόδανθι agreeing with a vocative Γόγγυλα, eliminating the separate addressee altogether; Edmonds further supplies Λύδα[ν] where Voigt/Campbell leave ἀ.[ ... πᾶ[κτιν as a separate, differently-restored phrase.

(3) OPENING VERB-PHRASE. Voigt/Campbell: ".]ε.[…. ].[ … κ]έλομαι σ᾿ ἀ̣[είδην". Edmonds (OCR, verbatim): "[Tui]$¢ μ[οι νύκ]τ[ος, κ]έλομαί σ᾽, ἄπελθε," — a substantially different conjectural supplement following the securely-read κέλομαι σ(ε).

(4) WHERE THE PAPYRUS IS BEST PRESERVED, the two recensions substantially agree, differing mainly in accentuation/breathing conventions and in how small gaps are filled: Voigt/Campbell "τὰν κάλαν· ἀ γὰρ κατάγωγις αὔτ̣α[ς σ᾿ / ἐπτόαισ᾿ ἴδοισαν, ἐγὼ δὲ χαίρω· / καὶ γαρ αὔτ̣α δήπο[τ᾿] ἐμέμφ[ετ᾿ ἄγνα / Κ]υπρογέν[ηα" vs. Edmonds (OCR, verbatim): "τὰν κάλαν' ἀ γὰρ κατάγωγις αὔτα / ἐπτόαισ᾽ ἴδοισαν,3 ἔγω δὲ χαίρω. / καὶ γὰρ αὔτα δή πἰοτ᾽] ἐμεμφ[όμαν τὰν / [K]umpoyér[nav:]" (the last word is OCR-garbled but is evidently the same κ-word ending -ρογέν- as in Voigt/Campbell). This agreement in the securely-legible stretch, against divergence in the lacunose stretches, is itself a useful indicator of which parts of the papyrus are solid readings versus editorial supplement.

(5) The remainder of Edmonds' text (his lines corresponding to Voigt/Campbell's ὠ̣ς ἄραμα̣[ι / τοῦτο τὦ[πος / β]όλλομα̣[ι) is also given only in heavily conjectural, differently-worded form; given the OCR reliability concerns noted above, it is reported under 'witnesses' rather than repeated in full detail here.

Confidence is high for the primary (Voigt/Campbell) text: it was fetched directly and verified against the raw HTML of digitalsappho.org, where each Greek line is individually marked up (lang="grc"), and the page's own source-note cites P.Oxy. 1231 frr. 12 and 15 and Campbell's 1982 Loeb (itself following Voigt 1971) — this is the text given in greek_text.

The secondary (Edmonds 1922) recension was retrieved only as the DjVu OCR text layer of an archive.org scan; OCR of polytonic Greek on that scan is demonstrably imperfect in places (Greek letters occasionally rendered as similar-looking Latin letters). I have quoted it exactly as fetched (per the task's verbatim requirement) and flagged, rather than silently "corrected," the corrupted spots; a fully reliable transcription would require checking the actual page image (archive.org items in.ernet.dli.2015.43750 or lyragraecavolume00edmo_534, printed page 215) rather than the OCR text, which I was not able to do within this session (archive.org's search-inside/page-image APIs did not return usable results for this item in the time available).

I searched (but did not find) any independent ancient quoting-author witness (e.g. in Athenaeus, Hephaestion, or a lexicographer such as Hesychius/Photius citing the rare word κατάγωγις) for this poem; the search was not exhaustive of the full TLG/lexicographic corpus, so I cannot rule out the existence of such a testimonium with certainty, but on current evidence the fragment appears to be preserved solely on this papyrus.

Per the task's absolute rule, all English-language translation text present on the fetched pages (including a full running English translation on the Edmonds/Lyra Graeca page and on the digitalsappho.org vocabulary-gloss table) was identified and deliberately excluded from this output; only Greek text and bibliographic/philological citation material appear above.

1. This fragment is a 20th-century papyrological discovery, not a fragment preserved by any ancient quoting author; it is attested only by two independent papyri (P.Oxy. 1231 and P.Oxy. 2166(a)), so no "testimonium" witness exists to compare against the papyri.

2. The text is heavily lacunose (each line breaks off in a gap, marked "[" ), and roughly a third of the words shown above are editorial restorations bridging holes in the papyrus rather than surviving ink; I have preserved editors' square brackets, dots, and other diacritical marks exactly as given in the fetched sources to keep restored vs. attested letters distinguishable.

3. I could not independently locate a freely fetchable scan/transcription of the P.Oxy. 2166(a) ed. princeps itself (Lobel, Oxyrhynchus Papyri vol. XVIII, 1941, with addenda in vol. XXI, 1951) — that publication appears to sit behind institutional/print access. Its readings are represented here at second hand via (a) Voigt's 1971 composite critical edition (as reproduced on digitalsappho.org) and (b) Michele Gorini's independent re-transcription from photographs of the papyrus (both cited above). Direct verification against Lobel's own published apparatus was not possible with the tools available in this session.

4. The task's description mentions "nightingale imagery," but no form of ἀηδών ("nightingale") appears anywhere in any witness or recension of this fragment that I was able to locate. The papyrological identification of "fragment 27" (Lobel-Page/Voigt numbering) as the wedding-occasion poem addressed to a girl "who was once a child," with imperative summons to companions and explicit mention of a γάμος ("wedding," στείχομεν γὰρ ἐς γάμον) and παρθένοι ("maidens," παρθένοις ἄπεμπε), is well supported and cross-checked against three independent modern sources (digitalsappho.org/Voigt, the 1914 Grenfell–Hunt editio princeps, and Gorini's independent re-transcription); but nightingale imagery does not occur in it under any numbering system I checked. That motif belongs to other Sappho fragments (e.g. the separate poem on P.Oxy. 1231 fr. 56, immediately following in the same papyrus roll = Voigt/L-P fr. 30, a night-vigil poem for a bride, likewise without an explicit nightingale word in what survives; or the single verse fr. 136, ἦρος ἄγγελος ἰμερόφωνος ἀήδων, not researched here as it was not the requested fragment). I have not included fr. 30 or fr. 136 material in the Greek text above since the task named fragment 27 specifically; this discrepancy in the task's own description is flagged here rather than silently resolved by substituting a different fragment.

5. Per the task's absolute rule, no English rendering, paraphrase, or summary of Sappho's Greek words is included anywhere above; all English is limited to bibliographic/technical description of the papyri and editions.

sourced.greek_text:
NOTE ON TRANSMISSION: This poem has, in the strict sense, a SINGLE ultimate ancient witness — the quotation embedded in [Longinus], Περὶ ὕψους / De Sublimitate ("On the Sublime") 10.1–3, transmitted solely through the medieval Byzantine manuscript tradition of that treatise (chiefly the 10th-century Codex Parisinus Graecus 2036, siglum "P", with later apographs). No independent papyrus of the poem itself is known. Because different modern editors resolve the manuscripts' corruptions differently, four independently fetched recensions of that one witness are given below verbatim, each as printed/digitized in its own edition, followed by a fifth (Digital Sappho) given only for cross-check since it is a modern website rather than a listed primary-source type. Line-division into Sapphic stanzas follows the verse-lineation actually shown on the page images consulted (Wharton, Edmonds); where a source (Perseus) displays the passage as running prose without preserved verse-lineation, the same conventional four-line stanza division is applied for legibility, as a formatting choice only — no wording is altered.

=== RECENSION 1 — [Longinus], On the Sublime 10.2, ed. William Rhys Roberts (Cambridge University Press, 1907), digitized text, Perseus Digital Library (Perseus:text:2008.01.0639:chapter=10) ===

φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θεοῖσιν
ἔμμεν ὡνήρ, ὅστις ἐναντίος τοι
ἱζάνει καὶ πλησίον ἁδὺ φωνεύσας
ὑπακούει

καὶ γελαίσας ἱμερόεν, τό μοι μὰν
καρδίαν ἐν στήθεσιν ἐπτόασεν·
ὥς σε γὰρ ἴδω βροχέως, με φωνᾶς
οὐδὲν ἔτ᾽ εἴκει·

ἀλλὰ κὰμ μὲν γλῶσσα ἔαγε, λεπτὸν
δ᾽ αὐτίκα χρῶ πῦρ ὑπαδεδρόμακεν,
ὀππάτεσσι δ᾽ οὐδὲν ὅρημ᾽, ἐπιρρόμ-
βεισι δ᾽ ἄκουαι.

κὰδ δέ μ᾽ ἱδρὼς κακχέεται, τρόμος δὲ
παῖσαν ἀγρεῖ, χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας
ἐμμί, τεθνάκην δ᾽ ὀλίγω ᾽πιδεύην
φαίνομαι.

ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα ...

=== RECENSION 2 — H. T. Wharton, "Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings, and a Literal Translation" (London, 1885; text "following Bergk's edition"), fragment 2, transcribed here from the Project Gutenberg e-text (#57390) of Wharton's book, raw HTML entities decoded and verified byte-for-byte ===

Φαίνεταί μοι κήνος ἴσος θέοισιν
ἔμμεν ὤνηρ, ὄστις ἐναντίος τοι
ἰζάνει, καὶ πλασίον ἆδυ φωνεύ-
σας ὑπακούει

καὶ γελαίσας ἰμερόεν, τό μοι μάν
καρδίαν ἐν στήθεσιν ἐπτόασεν·
ὡς γὰρ εὔιδον βροχέως σε, φώνας
οὐδὲν ἔτ' εἴκει·

ἀλλὰ κὰμ μὲν γλῶσσα ἔαγε, λέπτον δ'
αὔτικα χρῷ πῦρ ὐπαδεδρόμακεν,
ὀππάτεσσι δ' οὐδὲν ὄρημ', ἐπιρρόμ-
βεισι δ' ἄκουαι.

ἀ δέ μίδρως κακχέεται, τρόμος δέ
παῖσαν ἄγρει, χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας
ἔμμι, τεθνάκην δ' ὀλίγω 'πιδεύης
φαίνομαι [ἄλλα].

ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον, [ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα].

Φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν
ἔμμεν ὤνηρ, ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι

σας ὐπακούει

ὡς γὰρ ἔς τ' ἴδω, Βρόχε', ὤς με φώνας

φαίνομαι· — ἀλλὰ

πάντ<α νῦν τ>ολμάτε', ἐπεὶ πένησα.
[lacuna/break — Longinus's own prose resumes]

sourced.variants:
Because the poem survives through one quoted exemplar read differently by successive editors, the recensions above diverge at several well-known cruces. Line references are to the stanza layout above (stanza.line).

(1) NUMBERING: This fragment is Bergk's/Wharton's/Edmonds's "fr. 2" but the now-standard citation, used by Lobel-Page (1955), Voigt (1971), Campbell (Loeb 1982), aoidoi.org, Digital Sappho and Wikipedia, is "fr. 31" (Lobel-Page/Voigt numbering, which incorporates the papyrus finds and renumbered the whole corpus). Both numbers denote the same poem.

(2) 1.2 ὅστις/ὄστις/ὄττις: Rhys Roberts prints the Atticized ὅστις (rough breathing, single τ); Wharton/Bergk ὄστις (smooth breathing, single τ); Edmonds and the Lobel-Page-based text both give the fully Aeolic geminate ὄττις.

(3) 1.3 ἱζάνει/ἰζάνει/ἰσδάνει: Rhys Roberts and Wharton print ἰζάνει/ἱζάνει (ζ); Edmonds also ἰζάνει; the aoidoi (Moore/Campbell) and Digital Sappho (Lobel-Page) texts print the alternative Aeolic spelling ἰσδάνει (σδ for ζ) — an orthographic rather than substantive difference.

(4) 1.3 πλησίον/πλάσιον: Rhys Roberts alone prints the Atticized πλησίον (η); all four other recensions print the Aeolic πλάσιον (ᾱ).

(5) 2.1 τό μοι μὰν / τό μοι μάν / τὸ δὴ 'μαν / τό μ' ἦ μάν: this word-group is the first major crux. Rhys Roberts and Wharton/Bergk independently agree on τό μοι μάν(v); aoidoi (Moore/Campbell) and Digital Sappho (Lobel-Page) independently agree on τό μ' ἦ μάν; Edmonds prints τὸ δὴ 'μαν, explicitly following the 19th-century philologist Ahrens's conjecture, and states in his apparatus (n.1, p.186) that "the mss[read] μὴ μάν."

(6) 2.2 καρδίαν ... ἐπτόασεν / ἐπτόησεν / κάρζαν ... ἐπεπτόασεν: Rhys Roberts and Wharton/Bergk both read καρδίαν ... ἐπτόασεν; aoidoi (Moore/Campbell) and Digital Sappho (Lobel-Page) both read καρδίαν ... ἐπτόησεν; Edmonds substitutes the rare word κάρζαν for καρδίαν and prints ἐπεπτόασεν, crediting the conjecture to Robortelli/himself and stating in his apparatus (n.2) that "mss [read] καρδίαν ἐν στήθεσσιν (-εσιν) ἐπτόασεν (corr. in one [ms] to ἐποπτόασεν)" — i.e. even Edmonds's own apparatus confirms the plain manuscript reading is καρδίαν ... ἐπτόασεν, with one manuscript instead correcting to ἐποπτόασεν.

(7) 3.1–3.2 (the "briefly I see you" line) — the most contested crux in the poem: Rhys Roberts prints ὥς σε γὰρ ἴδω βροχέως, με φωνᾶς; Wharton/Bergk prints ὡς γὰρ εὔιδον βροχέως σε, φώνας; aoidoi (Moore/Campbell) and Digital Sappho (Lobel-Page) both print ὡς/ὠς γὰρ εἰσίδω βροχέως σε, φώνας. Edmonds diverges most sharply, splitting the adverb βροχέως into a vocative proper name addressed to the beloved, "Βρόχε(α)" (a supposed pet-name, from βραχύς), printing ὡς γὰρ ἔς τ' ἴδω, Βρόχε', ὤς με φώνας — his footnote (n.1, p.187) glosses this as "(or Brochea) dimin. of a compd. of βραχύς," and his footnote on the same line (n.3) states "mss [read] ὥς γ[ὰρ] σίδω βρόχεως (βροχέως) κ.τ.λ.," i.e. Edmonds's own apparatus shows the manuscript reading is the corrupt σίδω against a plain adverb βρόχεως, and that his "Βρόχε'"-as-name reading is his own idiosyncratic construal, not shared by any other edition consulted here.

(8) 4.2 ὑπαδεδρόμακεν / ὐπαδεδρόμηκεν: Rhys Roberts, Wharton/Bergk, and Edmonds all print the (unaugmented) perfect ὑπαδεδρόμακεν/ὐπαδεδρόμακεν (differing only in breathing); aoidoi (Moore/Campbell) and Digital Sappho (Lobel-Page) print the augmented ὑπαδεδρόμηκεν/ὐπαδεδρόμηκεν.

(9) 5.1 κὰδ δέ μ' ἴδρως κακχέεται / ἀ δέ μ' ἴδρως κακχέεται / ψῦχρος-variants: Rhys Roberts alone keeps κάδ (= κατά, "down"); Wharton/Bergk, Edmonds, aoidoi and Digital Sappho all print ἀ/καδ instead (a feminine article/demonstrative before ἴδρως). More importantly, aoidoi's apparatus (n.13, citing its two base editions by name) records: "κακχέεται Moore : ψῦχρος ἔχει Campbell" — i.e. Moore (1947) prints κακχέεται ("pours down") where Campbell (1967) prints the different phrase ψῦχρος ἔχει ("cold holds/seizes") at this same point. Independently, Edmonds's apparatus (n.6, p.187) reports that an editor he abbreviates "Long." "apparently read κὰδ δ' ἴδρως ψῦχρος χέεται," reporting that editor's manuscripts as giving "ἐκ δὲ (ἐκαδε) μ' ἰδ. ψ. κακχέεται," and Edmonds argues μοι is grammatically necessary. All three of these independent apparatus notes (aoidoi/Moore/Campbell; Edmonds/"Long.") converge on the same real crux: this line is corrupt in the manuscript(s), and editors differ over whether it read a form of κακχέεται alone or involved ψῦχρος ("cold").

(10) 5.2 ἀγρεῖ / ἄγρει / ἄγρη: minor verb-ending variation across the same word (Rhys Roberts ἀγρεῖ; Wharton, aoidoi, Digital Sappho ἄγρει; Edmonds ἄγρη).

(11) 5.3 ᾽πιδεύην / 'πιδεύϝην / 'πιδεύης: Rhys Roberts and Wharton both give (ὀλίγω) ᾽πιδεύην/'πιδεύης without a digamma; aoidoi and Digital Sappho give 'πιδεύης; Edmonds alone marks a digamma, 'πιδεύϝην, and his apparatus (n.7, p.187) reports "mss [give] πιδευσην, πιδευην, or πιδευκην" — i.e. he documents three different actual manuscript spellings/corruptions at this word.

(12) End of poem — the text becomes lacunose/uncertain in every recension, and this is where the divergence is greatest: Rhys Roberts prints continuous ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα ... with no brackets; Wharton/Bergk prints ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον, [ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα]. with the last three words bracketed as a supplement; aoidoi gives only ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον ... and stops, noting in prose (not apparatus number) that "the last part of the fourth strophe is completely muddled... I have omitted what is probably the final word of the strophe," and that a following three-word "fifth strophe" (not shown in the fetched excerpt) "may not belong in this poem at all, but [is] included in standard editions." Edmonds diverges completely, printing πάντ<α νῦν τ>ολμάτε', ἐπεὶ πένησα — an imperative "τολμάτε'" governing a new syntax — and his apparatus (n.8, p.187) states "mss [give] ἀ. παντόλματον ἐ. (ἐ. καί) πένητα," i.e. the actual manuscript reading (confirmed independently by Rhys Roberts's plain text ἀλλὰ πᾶν τολματόν/παντόλματον ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα) is close to what Rhys Roberts and Wharton print, and Edmonds's rewriting to a 2nd-person imperative is his own emendation against that manuscript reading.

NOT included as Greek-text witnesses: (a) Catullus, Carmen 51, a close Latin adaptation of this ode — mentioned by Wharton's edition as evidence bearing on a possible lost final stanza, but it is composed in Latin, not Greek, and per the task's rules no Latin or English rendering of it is reproduced here; (b) Plutarch, who according to Wharton's introductory note (not the Greek text itself) alludes to/praises this ode ("mixed with fire") — no fetched source in this research produced actual Greek words of Sappho fr. 31 quoted by Plutarch, so he is not counted as a textual witness here; (c) an early-3rd-century-AD papyrus commentary sometimes cited in secondary literature as P.Oxy. 2506 (= Voigt fr. 213B), reported by some web sources to discuss/quote fr. 31 — see caveats, this could not be independently verified from a primary source in this research and is therefore NOT included as a confirmed witness.
sourced.caveats:
1. SOLE PRIMARY WITNESS: In the strict philological sense there is only one ancient witness to this poem — its quotation in [Longinus], On the Sublime 10.1–3, surviving via a single medieval manuscript line (Parisinus Graecus 2036 and its apographs). No papyrus of Sappho fr. 31 has been confirmed in this research. Several web-search result summaries (not the pages actually fetched) falsely claimed that P.Oxy. 2288 preserves fr. 31 — this is incorrect; P.Oxy. 2288 belongs to Sappho fr. 1 ("Ode to Aphrodite"), a different poem, as one of the summaries itself then went on to confirm. A separate search-summary claim that the Berlin parchment P.Berol. 9722 preserves fr. 31 was checked directly against the English Wikipedia "Sappho 31" article and found to be unsupported there; other sources place P.Berol. 9722 with fr. 94–96 (a different part of the corpus), not fr. 31. Both claims are flagged as search-summarization errors and are NOT relied on above.

2. POSSIBLE SECOND ANCIENT WITNESS, UNVERIFIED: secondary/tertiary web material (not a primary source actually fetched) mentions "fr. 213B" in Voigt's edition as a c. 3rd-century-AD papyrus commentary bearing on fr. 31 (possibly identical with, or related to, P.Oxy. 2506, a papyrus commentary on lyric poetry sometimes discussed under the heading "Dark Sappho"). This could not be confirmed from a directly fetched primary source with quotable Greek text in the time available, so it is not included above as a citable witness; it is flagged here so a follow-up researcher can pursue it (e.g. via Voigt's 1971 apparatus or a papyrological database) rather than treating the poem's transmission as fully closed.

3. OCR RELIABILITY: the archive.org OCR (djvu.txt) of the Edmonds 1922 volume is badly garbled for the Greek font used (Greek letters are frequently substituted with lookalike Latin characters). Rather than transcribe that garbled text, the relevant pages (pp. 185–187 of the printed book) were located, rendered to PNG images locally at 300dpi using PyMuPDF (poppler-utils was unavailable and could not be installed in this environment), and read visually — this is the same method used for the aoidoi.org PDF, whose text layer is also not cleanly machine-extractable. Both are reported above as directly read from a legible page image, not blind OCR.

4. NO ENGLISH RENDERING INCLUDED: per the task's absolute rule, no English (or other modern-language) translation of Sappho's words appears anywhere above. English is used only for bibliographic citation and for describing textual-critical facts (which editor conjectured what, what the manuscripts are reported to read) — never to render what any Greek word or line means. Some fetched pages (e.g. Wharton's own book, which prints a facing literal prose translation, and Gladstone's/Burton's verse translations of Catullus's Latin) were deliberately not quoted from, precisely to keep translation out of this output.

5. STANZA LINEATION: Perseus's Rhys Roberts text is delivered as running prose (word-linked for morphological lookup) rather than with preserved verse line-breaks; I imposed the conventional four-line-Sapphic-stanza lineation on it (matching how the same words are lineated in the Wharton and Edmonds page images) purely as a formatting/legibility choice — no words were added, removed, or reordered from what was fetched.

6. This research task was scoped to the Greek text and its ancient/editorial witnesses only; no assessment is offered here of modern reconstruction theories (e.g., Armand D'Angour's proposed 8-stanza reconstruction, mentioned only in a Wikipedia summary and not independently pursued) since those go beyond quoting/witnessing the transmitted ancient text.
sourced.note: The 'he seems to me equal to the gods' poem — first-person catalog of physical symptoms on watching a beloved woman with a man; quoted whole by [Longinus], On the Sublime.

witnesses.source: Eustathius of Thessalonica, Commentarii ad Homeri Iliadem, on Iliad Θ (8).552–555 (ad loc. φαεινὴν ἀμφὶ σελήνην), standardly cited as 'Eust. 729.20'
witnesses.edition: Ed. G. Stallbaum, Commentarii ad Homeri Iliadem, vol. 2 (Leipzig, 1827–30) — OCR text from Internet Archive scan; passage located at the point commenting on the Homeric simile ἀστέρα φαεινὴν ἀμφὶ σελήνην (Il. 8.555), internal page marked '231' in this scan (=734/729 in the traditional running pagination cited by modern scholarship)
witnesses.note: Direct quotation introduced by 'χαϑὰ καὶ ἡ Σαπφώ που φησίν' ('as Sappho too somewhere says'). Gives three clauses only, ending at γᾶν; does not continue with ἀργυρία or any 'silver' word. Manuscript/print tradition of Eustathius' own text is Attic/koine-flavored rather than pure Aeolic (ἀποκρύπτουσι, ὁπότ᾽ ἄν, καλάν σελάναν, φαεινὸν εἶδος), which modern editors 'Aeolicize' when constructing a critical text of Sappho (see variants).

witnesses.source: Julian (Emperor), Epistulae, Letter 194, addressed Ἰουλιανὸς Ἐκηβολίῳ ('Julian to Hecebolius'); classified by its editors among the 'Epistulae vel Dubiae' (letters of doubtful authenticity)
witnesses.edition: Julian, Epistulae, leges, poematia, fragmenta varia, ed. J. Bidez & F. Cumont (Paris/London, 1922), pp. 264–265 (section 'IV. Epistulae Spuriae... Vel Dubiae') — OCR text from Internet Archive scan
witnesses.note: Not a verbatim quotation of Sappho's verse: Julian reports in indirect discourse that 'the beautiful Sappho' (Σαπφὼ ἡ καλή) called the moon ἀργυρέαν ('silver') and says this is why it hides (ἀποκρύπτειν) the sight of the other stars. The editors' apparatus at this point reads: '10 sq. Sapph. Fr. 3. Cf. Iulian. 109 C' — i.e. they identify this as a reference to the same Sappho fragment numbered 3 in Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci (= fr. 34 in Diehl/Lobel-Page/Voigt/Campbell numbering), and cross-reference another passage in Julian's own corpus (p. 109C of the standard Julian pagination) making a similar gold/silver-sun/moon comparison.

witnesses.source: H. T. Wharton, Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings, and a Literal Translation, 3rd ed. (London, 1895; text as given in the Project Gutenberg e-text of this public-domain edition) — fragment numbered '3' by Wharton, following Bergk's numbering; = fr. 34 Lobel-Page/Voigt/Campbell
witnesses.edition: Project Gutenberg e-text #57390 (transcribed from Wharton's printed Greek, including his editorial diacritics/brackets)
witnesses.note: Composite/critical text, not an independent ancient witness: merges the Eustathius quotation (Aeolicized) with the word ἀργυρία placed conjecturally in a metrical gap after γᾶν on the strength of Julian's testimony to Sappho's epithet 'silver' — a placement Wharton attributes to a suggestion of Bishop Blomfield. Wharton's page also states (in English, as bibliographic/source information, not as any rendering of Sappho's Greek) that the fragment was 'Quoted by Eustathius of Thessalonica, late in the twelfth century, to illustrate the simile in the Iliad, viii. 551' and that 'Julian, about 350 A.D., says Sappho applied the epithet silver to the moon; wherefore Blomfield suggested its position here.'

sourced.variants:
Two genuinely independent ancient witnesses exist, and they do not overlap in wording at all — Eustathius quotes verse-text, Julian only paraphrases a single epithet — so the 'variants' below are of two different kinds: (A) real transmissional variants within/around the Eustathius quotation, and (B) the editorial reconciliation modern scholars perform to combine the two witnesses into one composite fragment.

(A) Within the Eustathius quotation:
1. The adverb before the verb (meaning roughly 'straightway'/'back again') is transmitted unstably across manuscripts and printed editions of Eustathius' Commentary: forms reported in modern apparatus include ἂψ, αἶψ, and ἆιψ. My OCR of the Stallbaum-edition scan rendered this word illegibly/corruptly (as 'dy'), so I could not independently resolve which of these three the scan actually prints; this should be checked against a clean facsimile or a modern critical apparatus (e.g. Voigt's or Campbell's) rather than relied on from my OCR pass.
2. Eustathius' own quoted Greek is markedly less 'Aeolic' than the form usually printed as Sappho fr. 34 in modern editions (Bergk, Wharton, Lobel-Page, Voigt, Campbell): Eustathius' text gives ἀποκρύπτουσι, ὁπότ᾽ ἄν, καλάν σελάναν (single -ν-), φαεινὸν εἶδος; the standard modern critical text instead prints the Aeolicized forms ἀπυκρύπτοισι, ὄπποτα, κάλαν σελάνναν (geminate -νν-), φάεννον εἶδος. This is a systematic editorial normalization to Sappho's Aeolic dialect, not something attested word-for-word in Eustathius himself — i.e. the 'Sapphic-looking' Aeolic text everyone quotes is itself a modern scholarly reconstruction laid over Eustathius' more Attic/koine-flavored quotation.

(B) Reconciling Eustathius and Julian:
3. Eustathius' quotation ends cleanly after γᾶν ('earth'/'land'), with nothing following in his text. Julian never quotes any Sapphic verse-words at all — he only states, in his own prose and indirect discourse, that Sappho called the moon ἀργυρέαν ('silver'). Modern composite editions (represented here by Wharton 1885) splice the two together: they keep Eustathius' three lines verbatim (Aeolicized), then add the bracketed conjecture [ἐπὶ πᾶσαν] and insert the word ἀργυρία (the Aeolic equivalent of Julian's ἀργυρέαν) into an assumed metrical lacuna after γᾶν, marking the surrounding gap with meter-filler symbols. Neither addition is transmitted continuous text from any single ancient source; it is an editorial reconstruction (traced by Wharton to a suggestion of Bishop Blomfield) built by combining the two independent witnesses.
4. Fragment numbering differs by edition: Bergk (Poetae Lyrici Graeci) and Wharton (following Bergk) both number this fragment '3'; the Bidez–Cumont apparatus to Julian likewise cites it as 'Sapph. Fr. 3' (i.e. Bergk's numbering); modern standard numbering (Diehl, Lobel–Page, Voigt, Campbell/Loeb) instead calls it fragment 34 — the number given in the task prompt.
sourced.caveats:
1. No papyrus witness for this fragment was found or is known to me from what I fetched; both ancient sources located are literary quotations/testimonia (Eustathius, 12th c. CE; Julian [or a letter transmitted under his name], 4th c. CE, itself only securely known through a 1922 critical edition of a medieval manuscript tradition), not a papyrus discovery. If a papyrus fragment overlapping this text exists, I did not locate it in this search session.
2. The Eustathius passage was extracted from an OCR'd 19th-century scan (Stallbaum's edition) on archive.org; Greek OCR of this kind of dense Byzantine commentary text is error-prone, especially for accents, breathings, and certain letterforms (σ/ς, θ/ϑ, and especially the short adverb before ἀποκρύπτουσι, which I could not resolve with confidence — see variant note A1 above). The passage's content and position (immediately following, and explicitly illustrating, Eustathius' comment on the Homeric lemma φαεινὴν ἀμφὶ σελήνην at Iliad 8.552–555) leaves little doubt this is the correct passage, but the exact letter-by-letter transcription of the adverb and of accent placement should be checked against a clean modern edition or facsimile rather than trusted from my OCR pass alone.
3. I was not able to independently verify the precise page/line locator 'Eust. 729.20' conventionally cited in modern Sappho scholarship against the archive.org scan I used (whose own internal pagination reads '231' at this point, evidently a different pagination scheme than the traditional running numbers reproduced in other editions of Eustathius); I am relying on content-matching, not on confirming that exact numeral.
4. The Julian letter (Ep. 194 Bidez–Cumont) is itself classified by its own modern editors as being of doubtful authenticity ('Epistulae vel Dubiae') — i.e., its attribution to the historical emperor Julian is not fully certain according to the edition I consulted; this affects how much independent weight this second 'witness' carries, though it does not affect the fact that a real ancient/late-antique or Byzantine source under Julian's name attests the word ἀργυρέαν applied by Sappho to the moon.
5. All bibliographic/source-identification information above is given in English because it describes editions, page numbers, and manuscript facts — this is not, and does not contain, any translation, paraphrase, or rendering into English (or any modern language) of Sappho's own words. No such translation appears anywhere in this output. The one piece of connected English prose quoted (from Wharton, in witness note III) is Wharton's own bibliographic/attribution note about who quotes the fragment and why — again not a translation of Sappho's Greek.
