[Witness: Demetrius, Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας (De Elocutione) §106 — manuscript text (cod. Paris. gr. 1741 = P), as printed by W. Rhys Roberts, 1902, p. 120]

ὑπηρετεῖ μὲν ἡ τοιάδε,

οἵαν τὰν ὑάκινθον ἐν οὔρεσι ποιμένες ἄνδρες
ποσσὶ καταστείβουσιν,

ἐπικοσμεῖ δὲ τὸ ἐπιφερόμενον τὸ
χαμαὶ δέ τε πορφύρον ἄνθος·

[Same witness, alternative modern recension of the second colon — Bergk's text, as printed by H. T. Wharton (1885/1895), fr. 94, following Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci⁴]

Οἴαν τὰν ὑάκινθον ἐν οὔρεσι ποίμενες ἄνδρες
πόσσι καταστείβοισι, χάμαι δ᾽ ἐπιπορφύρει ἄνθος.

witnesses.source: Demetrius, Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας / De Elocutione ("On Style") §106
witnesses.edition: W. Rhys Roberts (ed.), Demetrius On Style: The Greek Text of Demetrius De Elocutione (Cambridge University Press, 1902), p. 120
witnesses.note: This is the SOLE ancient witness for the fragment; it survives only as a literary quotation in Demetrius, not on papyrus. Demetrius quotes it anonymously, in two separate cola, as a rhetorical example (of a plain statement, and of an added 'epiphoneme' that adorns it); he does not name Sappho. The text is transmitted through a single manuscript, Codex Parisinus Graecus 1741 (siglum P). Roberts prints the P reading literatim, including the non-Aeolic verb-ending -ουσιν and the nominal (verbless) second colon.

witnesses.source: H. T. Wharton, Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings and a Literal Translation (1885; later eds. 1887, 1895), fragment 94
witnesses.edition: Text as reproduced on Greek Wikisource (page 'Ύμνοι και Επιθαλάμια'), cross-checked against the Project Gutenberg e-text of the same book (no. 57390, transliterated Greek: 'Oian tan yakinthon en ouresi poimenes andres / possi katasteiboisi, chamai d' epiporphyrei anthos')
witnesses.note: Not an independent ancient witness — Wharton is reproducing Theodor Bergk's edited/emended text of the same single Demetrius passage (Bergk, Poetae Lyrici Graeci, 4th ed., Sappho fr. 94). Wharton's accompanying note states explicitly: 'Quoted by Demetrius, as an example of the ornament and beauty proper to a concluding sentence. Bergk first attributed the lines to Sappho' — i.e. the ancient source itself is anonymous; the ascription to Sappho is a modern (19th-c.) scholarly inference by Bergk.

witnesses.source: J. M. Edmonds (ed. & tr.), Lyra Graeca, vol. i (Loeb Classical Library, 1922), Sappho frr. 151 (Demetrius' discussion) and 152 (the verse itself)
witnesses.edition: Archive.org OCR text of the 1922 Loeb edition
witnesses.note: Again the same single Demetrius passage, not a new witness. Edmonds' critical apparatus (readable amid otherwise badly garbled Greek OCR in this scan) explicitly records the manuscript reading as distinct from his own printed text: 'mss χ. δὲ τε πόρφυρον ἄνθος' (i.e. mss χαμαὶ δὲ τε πόρφυρον ἄνθος), citing Longus, Poimenika (Daphnis and Chloe) 4.8 as a parallel for the compound-verb emendation he prints instead. This independently corroborates Roberts' P-reading and Bergk's emendation as reported above.

sourced.variants: There is only ONE ancient witness to this fragment (Demetrius, On Style/De Elocutione §106, via the single manuscript P = Codex Parisinus Graecus 1741); no papyrus or second quoting author has been located. The apparent "variants" are therefore modern editorial recensions of that one manuscript reading, not competing ancient traditions: (1) First colon — the ms./Roberts text has the non-Aeolic present-indicative ending ποσσὶ καταστείβουσιν; Bergk's Aeolic-normalized recension (followed by Wharton) reads πόσσι καταστείβοισι. (2) Second colon — this is the real crux. The manuscript P, as printed literatim by Roberts, has a verbless/nominal clause: χαμαὶ δέ τε πορφύρον ἄνθος ("and on the ground [is] the purple flower," πορφύρον construed as an adjective agreeing with ἄνθος). Bergk emended this to a finite compound verb, χάμαι δ᾽ ἐπιπορφύρει ἄνθος ("and the flower glows/turns purple on the ground"), a reading followed by Edmonds (1922), who justifies the ἐπι- compound by comparison with Longus, Daphnis and Chloe 4.8. Roberts' own explanatory note (p. 120, on line 16) records Bergk's alternative but flags a metrical objection: the emendation "involves the shortening of the υ." (3) Breathing/orthography — Roberts prints ὑάκινθον with rough breathing (as the ms. of a prose author, Demetrius, transmits it); the Aeolicizing editions (Bergk/Wharton) print it with smooth breathing/psilosis, consistent with regular Aeolic loss of aspiration, though the Wikisource/Gutenberg transcriptions consulted here do not consistently render the breathing mark. (4) Attribution — the ancient source itself never names the poet; the ascription to Sappho is a modern inference, first made by Bergk (explicitly noted by both Wharton and Roberts' commentary).
sourced.caveats: 1. No papyrus witness for this fragment was found in any source fetched; all three fetched sources agree it survives solely as a quotation embedded in Demetrius, On Style §106. If a papyrus attestation exists in later publications (e.g. an unpublished or very recent find), it was not located within this search. 2. The Bergk (Poetae Lyrici Graeci, vol. 3, 1882 ed., archive.org item poetaelyricigrae03berguoft) and part of the Edmonds (Lyra Graeca vol. 1, 1922, archive.org item lyragraecabeingr01edmouoft) OCR text is badly garbled for the Greek portions (Google/Internet Archive OCR frequently mis-renders polytonic Greek as pseudo-Latin gibberish in these old scans), so I did not attempt to quote Bergk's or Edmonds' full printed Greek couplet directly from those garbled OCR passages — only their apparatus/commentary notes, which happened to render legibly and are quoted verbatim above, plus Wharton's version of the same Bergk-derived text (which had clean Greek via Wikisource/Gutenberg) were used. 3. The equation of this fragment with 'Sappho 105(c) Lobel-Page / 105c Voigt' is based on content match (identical Greek verses, identical citation to Demetrius §106, identical textual crux) established from these fetched 19th/early-20th-century sources; the Lobel-Page numbering system itself (1955) postdates all three editions consulted, so no fetched source uses the '105c' numbering by name — that numbering is supplied from the task's own identification of the target fragment, not verified against a fetched Lobel-Page or Voigt edition. 4. Per the task's absolute rule, no English (or other modern-language) translation of Sappho's words has been included anywhere above, including in the witness/variant notes, even though the fetched pages (Roberts, Wharton, Edmonds) all print facing-page or accompanying English translations.
sourced.note: Simile of a hyacinth trampled underfoot by shepherds in the mountains; also numbered 105(c) in Lobel-Page.

sourced.greek_text:
[Witness A — Hephaestion, Ἐγχειρίδιον περὶ μέτρων καὶ ποιημάτων VII.1]
ὕψοι δὴ τὸ μέλαθρον
ἀείρετε, τέκτονες ἄνδρες·
Ὑμήναον,
γαμβρὸς ἔρχεται ἶσος Ἄρευι.

[Witness B — Demetrius, Περὶ ἑρμηνείας (De Elocutione) 148]
ὕψου δή, φησί, τὸ μέλαθρον
ἀέρατε τέκτονες·
γαμβρὸς εἰσέρχεται ἶσος Ἀρηϊ,
ἀνδρὸς μεγάλου πολλῷ μείζων,

[Witness B, continued — Demetrius, De Elocutione 146 (separate citation, same author/work, different chapter)]
πέρροχος ὡς ὄτ᾽ ἀοιδὸς ὁ Λέσβιος ἀλλοδαποῖσιν.

witnesses.source: Hephaestion, Ἐγχειρίδιον περὶ μέτρων καὶ ποιημάτων (Enchiridion), chapter VII §1 — cited there as παρὰ Σαπφοῖ (91), i.e. Sappho fr. 91 in Bergk's numbering, to illustrate the technical term μεσύμνιον ('intervening refrain'). Old (Westphal) pagination = p.132, marked in this edition's margin as [132].
witnesses.edition: Hephaestionis Enchiridion, cum commentariis veteribus, ed. Maximilianus Consbruch (Teubner, Leipzig, 1906)
witnesses.note: Quotes only three verses (= Voigt/L-P 111.1-3) plus the refrain Ὑμήναον; does NOT include the πέρροχος... line found in Demetrius. Consbruch's apparatus records ms sigla A, I (Ι), C, H.

witnesses.source: Demetrius, Περὶ ἑρμηνείας (De Elocutione / 'On Style') §§146 and 148 — two separate citations in two different chapters, illustrating two different rhetorical points (§146: χάρις from παραβολή/comparison; §148: χάρις from μεταβολή/self-correction). Footnotes in this edition mark them as Sappho, Fragm. 92, Bergk⁴ (§146) and Sappho, Fragm. 91, Bergk⁴ (§148) — i.e. Bergk treated them as two distinct fragments, not one continuous poem.
witnesses.edition: Demetrius on Style: the Greek text of Demetrius De Elocutione, ed. and tr. W. Rhys Roberts (Cambridge University Press, 1902), Greek text based on the sole manuscript P (Parisinus 1741)
witnesses.note: §148 opens with the narrating verb φησί ('she says') interjected by Demetrius, not part of Sappho's verse. §146's πέρροχος line is nowhere linked by Demetrius himself to the μέλαθρον lines; their combination into one poem is a modern editorial act (see variants).

sourced.variants:
Two independent ancient witnesses exist (no papyrus survives for this piece); no witness quotes the whole poem as now printed, and the two witnesses disagree on wording at nearly every point of overlap:

1. OPENING WORD: Both traditions are corrupt here and rest on editorial correction, not ms consensus.
   - Hephaestion mss: A reads ὕφοι, I (Ι) reads ὑψοῖ; Bergk's correction ὕψοι is what Consbruch prints (apparatus: "ὕψοι Bergk, ὕφοι (sic) A, ὑψοῖ Ι").
   - Demetrius ms P (the sole witness) reads the nonsensical νίψω; editors (edd.) correct to ὕψου (apparatus: "ὕψου] edd., νίψω P."). Note ὕψοι (Hephaestion, Aeolic-flavored) vs ὕψου (Demetrius, as edited) is itself a further difference in form.

2. THE VERB 'RAISE': Hephaestion mss disagree among themselves (C: ἀείρατε corrected to ἀείρετε; A: ἀείρεται; I: ἀείρατε) — Consbruch prints ἀείρετε. Richard Bentley conjectured the properly Aeolic form ἀέρρετε (geminate ρ, matching Sappho's own dialect); this form appears in no manuscript of either witness but is adopted by later editors (noted explicitly in Roberts' Demetrius commentary, which quotes H. Weir Smyth's Greek Melic Poets p.33 printing ἀέρρετε). Demetrius's ms P instead reads ἀέρατε (single ρ, Attic-flavored, no ms variation recorded here).

3. REFRAIN PLACEMENT: Hephaestion's manuscripts (codd.) add a second ὑμήναον immediately after μέλαθρον (i.e. duplicating the refrain within line 1); this is absent from Demetrius's quotation (deest ap. Demetr. de eloc. 148) and was deleted by the editor Westphal as intrusive.

4. "THE BRIDEGROOM APPROACHES, EQUAL TO ARES": Hephaestion: γαμβρὸς ἔρχεται ἶσος Ἄρευι (no εἰσ- prefix; Aeolic dative Ἄρευι for "Ares"; ms I reads ἄρει instead of Ἄρευι). Demetrius: γαμβρὸς εἰσέρχεται ἶσος Ἀρηϊ (with εἰσ- prefix "enters"; Attic/Ionic-flavored dative Ἀρηϊ). This εἰσέρχεται/ἔρχεται divergence is the most-discussed crux in the fragment's transmission.

5. "TALLER BY FAR THAN A BIG MAN": Hephaestion does not preserve this line at all (its quotation stops after the Ares line). Demetrius §148 alone preserves it, in Attic-normalized form: ἀνδρὸς μεγάλου πολλῷ μείζων (vs. the Aeolic ἄνδρος μεγάλω πόλυ μείζων printed by modern editors such as Smyth, again cited secondhand in Roberts' commentary).

6. THE 'ΠΕΡΡΟΧΟΣ' COUPLET (πέρροχος ὡς ὄτ᾽ ἀοιδὸς ὁ Λέσβιος ἀλλοδαποῖσιν): attested ONLY in Demetrius §146, a chapter apart from §148, illustrating a different stylistic point (comparison/παραβολή rather than self-correction/μεταβολή). Hephaestion never quotes it. Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci accordingly numbered the two passages as separate fragments (91 = §148's μέλαθρον lines; 92 = §146's πέρροχος line), as shown by the fragment numbers in the footnotes of Roberts' edition. Their fusion into a single continuous epithalamium (the basis of the now-standard Lobel-Page/Voigt fr. 111) is a later editorial construction — attested here indirectly via Roberts' commentary note quoting H. Weir Smyth's Greek Melic Poets (1900) p.33, which prints the two pieces run together with the refrain restored between every line, and via J. M. Edmonds' Lyra Graeca (1922), where the same construction appears as fr. 148 with a footnote explicitly stating "9-11 placed here from Demetr. El. 146" — i.e. the editor, not either ancient source, joins them.

In short: the only wording common to both ancient witnesses (τὸ μέλαθρον … ἀείρετε/ἀέρατε τέκτονες, and the Ares-comparison) is transmitted with real, ms-attested differences in preposition (ἔρχεται/εἰσέρχεται), dialect coloring (Ἄρευι/Ἀρηϊ, Aeolic vs. Attic forms throughout), and completeness (only Demetrius has the "ἀνδρὸς μεγάλου" line; only Demetrius has the πέρροχος couplet; only Hephaestion's tradition shows the duplicated-refrain corruption).
sourced.caveats:
1. No papyrus witness for this fragment is known to exist; both ancient sources are testimonia (metrical/rhetorical handbooks quoting Sappho as an illustrative example), not continuous-text papyri.

2. The Hephaestion text above is reconstructed by combining Consbruch's printed critical text with his own apparatus criticus, both fetched directly from the archive.org djvu.txt of his 1906 Teubner edition. The raw OCR of that scan garbles two words in the actual line (rendering ὕψοι as "ivo," and ἀείρετε as "ἀξίρετε"); I did not silently accept the OCR — I cross-checked and corrected only against Consbruch's own apparatus notes on the same fetched page (which explicitly discuss ὕψοι vs. ὕφοι/ὑψοῖ, and ἀείρετε vs. ἀείρατε/ἀείρεται), so every letter shown is sourced from the fetched document, not from memory. The Demetrius (Roberts 1902) OCR was clean Unicode Greek and required no such correction.

3. Two different archive.org scans of Demetrius's De Elocutione were tried; the Emory-scanned copy ("01067224.88908.emory.edu") had failed/garbled Greek OCR (zero real Greek Unicode recovered) and was abandoned in favor of the University-of-Toronto-scanned Roberts edition ("demetriusonstyle01deme"), which OCR'd cleanly.

4. I deliberately did NOT quote or use J. M. Edmonds' Lyra Graeca (1922), H. Weir Smyth's Greek Melic Poets (1900), or H. T. Wharton's Sappho (1885) as primary Greek text for the fragment itself, even though I located passages from/about them (via Roberts' 1902 commentary and Edmonds' own djvu.txt), because their combined/restored Aeolic text is a modern editorial synthesis of the two ancient citations rather than the wording of either ancient witness on its own; I report their existence and their fragment-numbering choices only in the variants section, for transparency about how the modern vulgate (Lobel-Page/Voigt fr. 111) was assembled.

5. The now-standard designation "fr. 111" is Lobel-Page/Voigt numbering (per the user's task description); the ancient/19th-century sources fetched here instead label it Bergk fr. 91 (Hephaestion's citation) / Bergk frr. 91 and 92 (Demetrius's two citations) — I did not independently verify a Voigt edition itself, since I could not locate an openly fetchable copy of Voigt's Sappho et Alcaeus (1971, still in copyright) online.

6. No modern-language translation of any Greek wording is included anywhere above; all bracketed labels are bibliographic (author/work/section citations), not renderings of Sappho's Greek.
sourced.note: Wedding hymn calling on carpenters to raise the roof-beam, comparing the bridegroom to Ares.

sourced.greek_text:
[Critical text — Hephaestion, Enchiridion 15.25 (ed. Consbruch), main text:]
ὄλβιε γαμβρέ, σοὶ μὲν δὴ γάμος, ὡς ἄραο,
ἐκτετέλεστ᾽, ἔχης δὲ παρθένον, ἂν ἄραο.

[Immediately following in the same source, cited separately as Sapph. 100 Bergk (Hephaestion, Ench. 15.26), belonging — per Hephaestion's own juxtaposition and per Wharton's note — to the same ode:]
μελλίχροος δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἱμερτῷ κέχυται προσώπῳ.

[Parallel transcription — H. T. Wharton's edition (his fragment 99) and Greek Wikisource "Επιγράμματα Σαπφούς" (Επίγραμμα 99), both following the ms.-I-based reading:]
Ὄλβιε γάμβρε, σοὶ μὲν δὴ γάμος ὡς ἄραο
ἐκτετέλεστ᾽, ἔχεις δὲ πάρθενον ἂν ἄραο.

witnesses.source: Hephaestion, Enchiridion de metris 15.25–26 (chapter Περὶ ἀσυναρτήτων), ed. Maximilianus Consbruch, Hephaestionis Enchiridion, cum commentariis veteribus (Teubner, 1906), p. 56
witnesses.edition: Consbruch's critical edition, scanned by HathiTrust/Google, hosted on archive.org
witnesses.note: The sole ancient testimonium for this couplet: Hephaestion quotes it, introduced as 'ἡ αὐτὴ ποιήτρια (Sapph. 99)' [i.e. Sappho, numbered 99 in the pre-Lobel-Page/Bergk-style numbering used by this edition and by 19th–early 20th c. scholarship; = fr. 112 in the modern Lobel-Page/Voigt/Campbell numbering], as an example of an asynartete (choriambic heptasyllabic + iambic clausula) meter. The immediately following line 'μελλίχροος δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἱμερτῷ κέχυται προσώπῳ' is cited a few lines later, separately introduced, as 'Sapph. 100'. Full manuscript apparatus for the first couplet given (see variants field).

witnesses.source: Henry Thornton Wharton, Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings, and a Literal Translation, fragment 99 (and 100)
witnesses.edition: London: John Lane, 1908 printing (2nd/later ed. text), Project Gutenberg eBook #57390
witnesses.note: Independent modern (public-domain, English-published) transcription of the same Hephaestion quotation. Wharton explicitly states both couplets (his frr. 99 and 100) are 'Quoted by Hephaestion ... to exemplify metres; both fragments seem to belong to the same ode.' Note: Gutenberg's plain-text transcription of this edition renders the Greek in italicized Latin transliteration ('[Greek: Olbie gambre, soi men dê gamos, ôs arao,] [Greek: ektetelest', echês de parthenon, an arao.]'); the Greek-script forms quoted above are cross-checked against Greek Wikisource's independent transcription of the identical text.

witnesses.source: Greek Wikisource, "Επιγράμματα Σαπφούς" ("Epigrams of Sappho"), Επίγραμμα 99 and Επίγραμμα 100
witnesses.edition: Wikisource (el), user-contributed transcription of the traditional/Bergk-numbered Sappho fragment corpus
witnesses.note: Gives the Greek in polytonic script directly (not transliterated), matching Wharton's fr. 99/100 numbering and wording almost exactly. Used to confirm the Greek-script form of the fragment independently of Consbruch's critical edition.

sourced.variants:
Because this fragment survives through a single ancient quoting source (Hephaestion's metrical handbook) rather than through multiple independent ancient authors or a papyrus, the 'witnesses' with genuine textual variation are the medieval manuscripts of Hephaestion himself, as recorded in Consbruch's apparatus criticus (sigla: A, C, P, I, H):

Line 1: accentuation of γαμβρέ/γάμβρε differs between the main text (γαμβρέ, oxytone) and ms. I (γάμβρε, paroxytone) — apparatus note "24 γάμβρε I". Wharton and Greek Wikisource both print the ms.-I form γάμβρε.

ἄραο: apparatus records a difference between ms. I and ms. A in accentuation/breathing ("ἄραο I, ἄραο A" as OCR'd — the scanned apparatus does not render the two forms' distinguishing diacritic clearly enough to be certain of the exact difference; flagged rather than guessed at).

Line 2 (ἐκτετέλεστ᾽, ...): 
- ἔχης (mss. C, P) vs ἔχηις (ms. A) vs ἔχεις (ms. I) — a three-way verb-form variant. Consbruch's main critical text prints ἔχης (following C, P); Wharton and Greek Wikisource both print ἔχεις (following ms. I).
- ἀνάραο (ms. I, i.e. crasis/univerbation of ἂν ἄραο) vs ἀναρᾶο (ms. A) — a word-division/accentuation variant for the same phrase.
- θ/ϑ (theta): Consbruch's Teubner typesetting uses the cursive-theta glyph ϑ throughout (παρϑένον); this is a font convention, not a textual variant, and is normalized to θ (παρθένον) in the Wharton/Wikisource transcriptions.

No papyrus witness to this fragment was located in this search, and none is known to survive; the fragment is not among the pieces recovered in P.Oxy., P.Sapph.Obbink, P.GC.inv.105, or the Berlin papyri collections searched.
sourced.caveats:
(1) Fragment-numbering caveat: the sources fetched here (Consbruch's Hephaestion, Wharton, Greek Wikisource) all use an older numbering convention that labels this couplet "Sappho 99" (and the following line "Sappho 100") rather than the modern Lobel-Page/Voigt/Campbell "fr. 112" cited in the task. I was unable, within this session's search-tool budget (the WebSearch tool's quota was exhausted before I could query it), to fetch a page that explicitly prints the label "fr. 112" next to this Greek text. The identification of this "ὄλβιε γάμβρε" couplet with modern fr. 112 rests on well-established, widely-cited classical scholarship (it is the standard, universally-recognized identification for this famous one-couplet wedding fragment) rather than on a freshly fetched page bearing that exact numeral — flagged here per the instruction to be transparent about anything uncertain in sourcing. The Greek text itself, by contrast, was verified against three independently fetched sources and is not reconstructed from memory.

(2) OCR caveat: the Consbruch apparatus criticus was read from an archive.org OCR'd scan (hephaestionisenc00hephuoft_djvu.txt) of a 1906 Teubner edition using antiquated font conventions (ϑ for θ, breathing/accent marks that OCR sometimes drops or garbles). Some apparatus entries (e.g. the exact form of the second "ἄραο" variant) could not be resolved with full confidence from the OCR text and are reported as uncertain rather than resolved by guesswork.

(3) Scope of "same ode" claim: Wharton's statement that the two couplets (his 99 and 100) "seem to belong to the same ode" is an editorial inference (his own, reported as such), not a claim made by Hephaestion himself, who cites them separately as two distinct metrical examples a few lines apart in his chapter Περὶ ἀσυναρτήτων.

(4) No English rendering, translation, or paraphrase of Sappho's Greek words appears anywhere above; all English text present is bibliographic/editorial description of the sources and apparatus only.
sourced.note: Wedding hymn praising the bridegroom's good fortune and the bride's grace.

Παρθενία, παρθενία, ποῖ με λίποισ᾽ ἀποίχῃ;
Οὐκέτι ἥξω πρὸς σέ, οὐκέτι ἥξω.

witnesses.source: Demetrius (Δημήτριος), Περὶ ἑρμηνείας / De Elocutione ("On Style"), §140 — the sole ancient testimonium quoting this fragment, cited by Demetrius as an example of ἀναδίπλωσις (reduplication) producing χάρις ("grace") in Sappho's style.
witnesses.edition: W. Rhys Roberts (ed.), Demetrius On Style: The Greek Text of Demetrius De Elocutione, edited after the Paris Manuscript, with Introduction, Translation, Facsimiles, etc. (Cambridge University Press, 1902), Greek text pp. 136–138, §140.
witnesses.note: This is the actual ancient-witness text, transmitted through a single medieval manuscript, Parisinus Graecus 1741 (siglum P — the book's title page states it is 'edited after the Paris manuscript'). Roberts's diplomatic text (verbatim from the fetched OCR, with only two obvious OCR letter-garbles silently resolved: 'wot'→ποῖ and 'TO'→τῷ, both confirmed by cross-checking the surrounding intact Greek and by witness 3 below) reads: '140. Αἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν σχημάτων χάριτες δῆλαί εἰσιν καὶ πλεῖσται παρὰ Σαπφοῖ, οἷον ἐκ τῆς ἀναδιπλώσεως, ὅπου νύμφη πρὸς τὴν παρθενίαν φησί, "παρθενία, παρθενία, ποῖ με λιποῦσα οἴχῃ;" ἡ δὲ ἀποκρίνεται πρὸς αὐτὴν τῷ αὐτῷ σχήματι, "οὐκέτι ἥξω πρὸς σέ, οὐκέτι ἥξω"· πλείων γὰρ χάρις ἐμφαίνεται, ἢ εἴπερ ἅπαξ ἐλέχθη καὶ ἄνευ τοῦ σχήματος. καίτοι ἀναδίπλωσις πρὸς δεινότητας μᾶλλον δοκεῖ εὑρῆσθαι, ἡ δὲ καὶ τοῖς δεινοτάτοις καταχρῆται ἐπιχαρίτως.' A footnote on the facing English page explicitly cites the couplet as 'Sappho, Fragm. 109, Bergk⁴.' The printed critical apparatus (verbatim from the fetched page) reads: '24 ὅπου εἀά. [= edd.]: ποῦ P. | παρθενείαν P. 24, 25 παρθενία alterum supra versum atram. evan. add. P.' — i.e. manuscript P actually reads ποῦ (not ὅπου), spells παρθενείαν (not παρθενίαν), and its second παρθενία was added later, above the line, in now-faded ink.

witnesses.source: H. T. Wharton, Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings and a Literal Translation, fragment 109 (Bergk's numbering).
witnesses.edition: 1st/2nd ed. (London, 1885/1887).

Wharton (1895), αποσπάσματα' (i.e. transcribed from Wharton's edition, 3rd ed. numbering, = Bergk 109 = modern/Lobel-Page-Voigt fr. 114).

witnesses.note:
Raw wikitext (verbatim as fetched): ':-Παρθενία, παρθενία, ποῖ με λίποισ᾽ ἀποίχῃ;
:-Οὐκέτι ἥξω πρὸς σέ, οὐκετι ἥξω.' The leading '-' marks are this edition's modern typographic device marking the two speaking parts (bride / Παρθενία personified), not part of the ancient text. Note the second 'οὐκετι' is printed without its accent in this specific transcription (an apparent transcription slip; the first occurrence is correctly accented οὐκέτι).

sourced.variants:
There is one ultimate ancient witness for this fragment — Demetrius, On Style §140 — surviving through a single medieval manuscript (Parisinus Graecus 1741, siglum P); no papyrus or second quoting author is known to preserve it. Two distinct recensions of the wording nonetheless circulate in scholarship, and both are attested in the fetched sources above:

(1) The diplomatic/manuscript-based text, printed by W. Rhys Roberts (1902) directly from P: λιποῦσα οἴχῃ ("having left, are you gone") — i.e. the participle λιποῦσα + finite οἴχῃ, in Koine/non-Aeolic morphology, exactly as the medieval scribe wrote it.

(2) The vulgate, Aeolic-restored text found in Bergk-derived editions (Wharton 1885/1895, and the Greek Wikisource transcription of Wharton): λίποισ' ἀποίχῃ — the Aeolic participle λίποισα (elided to λίποισ') governing ἀποίχῃ (compound with ἀπο-) instead of the simplex οἴχῃ. This is the standard modern editorial restoration (continued by Lobel-Page and Voigt) of Sappho's Aeolic dialect forms, on the assumption that Demetrius's prose-manuscript tradition had "corrected" Sappho's dialect spelling toward more familiar Koine forms when copying the quotation.

Additional apparatus-level variants within the sole manuscript witness P itself (per Roberts's critical apparatus, quoted in full in witness 1 above):
- Line "ὅπου νύμφη..." — the editors' ὅπου replaces the manuscript's actual reading ποῦ.
- P spells παρθενείαν (with extra ε) where the vulgate prints παρθενίαν.
- P's second occurrence of παρθενία (in "παρθενία, παρθενία") was not in the scribe's original line but was added afterward above the line, in ink that had faded by the time Roberts collated the manuscript.

Fragment-numbering variant (not a textual variant, but relevant to cross-referencing witnesses): this fragment is Bergk 109 (so numbered by Bergk, Wharton, and the Greek Wikisource transcription of Wharton) = the modern standard Lobel-Page/Voigt numbering fr. 114, which is the number under which the task identifies it.
sourced.caveats: All Greek quoted above was extracted from real fetched web/archive.org pages, not from memory; no English (or other modern-language) translation of Sappho's words is included anywhere in this output — English translations present on the fetched pages (by Wharton, by J. H. Merivale, and by Roberts) were seen but deliberately discarded, and only their bibliographic/attributive statements (e.g. "From Demetrius, who quotes the fragment...") were retained. No papyrus witness (P.Oxy., P.Sapph.Obbink, P.GC. inv. 105, Berlin papyri, etc.) is known or was found for this fragment; ancient transmission is exclusively through Demetrius's treatise via the single Paris manuscript P. The Wharton 1885/1887 archive.org OCR scan's Greek text is unreadable Latin-letter OCR garble (a font-recognition failure common on 19th-century books mixing Greek and English type) and was NOT used as a source of quoted Greek — it was used only for its (undamaged) English critical apparatus identifying the source as Demetrius. The Roberts 1902 Greek edition's OCR was largely clean, but two isolated single-word OCR misreads ('wot' for ποῖ, 'TO' for τῷ) were silently corrected in the quotation, since intervening/surrounding Greek in the same scan and the independent Wikisource witness both confirm the correct readings; this is flagged transparently rather than left as uncorrected garbage. I was not able to independently locate a fourth-party fetched source (e.g. Perseus Digital Library, TLG, a direct Bergk PLG scan) confirming the precise Demetrius section number beyond what Roberts's edition itself states, though Roberts's edition is itself the primary critical edition of that text and states the section number (140) directly. Web-search (WebSearch tool) was unavailable for this session (quota exhausted before this task began), so all sourcing here was done via direct WebFetch/curl retrieval of specific URLs rather than search-engine discovery; this may mean other legitimate witnesses or editions were not checked.

sourced.greek_text:
Ἔρος δαῦτέ μ᾽ ὁ λυσιμελὴς δόνει,
γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον. —
Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἔμεθεν μὲν ἀπήχθετο
φροντίσδην, ἐπὶ δ᾽ Ἀνδρομέδαν πότη.

witnesses.source: Hephaestion, Enchiridion (Ἐγχειρίδιον περὶ μέτρων), ch. VII § 7 — quoted as the example of the acatalectic Aeolic tetrameter, cited by the editor as "Sapph. 40" and "Sapph. 41"
witnesses.edition: Hephaestionis Enchiridion, cum commentariis veteribus, ed. Maximilianus Consbruch (Leipzig: Teubner, 1906), p. 23
witnesses.note: Primary/base ancient witness for both couplets, printed as running text with the couplets joined by a dash in Consbruch's edition. Base text follows cod. A (Ambrosianus I 8 ord. sup.) principally, against codd. D (Darmstadiensis 2773) and I (Parisinus 2676) — see variants.

witnesses.source: Anonymous Scholia B on Hephaestion's Enchiridion, Book III (on Aeolic dactylic verse), quoting the same two couplets again as (Sapph. 40. 41), each closed "(= Heph.)"
witnesses.edition: Hephaestionis Enchiridion, cum commentariis veteribus, ed. M. Consbruch (Leipzig: Teubner, 1906), p. 214
witnesses.note: Independent second occurrence of the same two couplets within the Hephaestion manuscript tradition, transmitted through a different scholiastic recension (ms. classes Y = codd. p,k; Z = third scholia class) with its own small divergences from the main Enchiridion text — see variants. Text as printed in this witness: 'Ἔρος δ᾽ αὖτέ μ᾽ ὁ λυσιμελὴς δονεῖ / γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον. --- / Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἔμεθεν μὲν ἀπήχθετο / φροντίσδην, ἐπὶ δ᾽ Ἀνδρομέδαν πότη.'

witnesses.source: H. T. Wharton, Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings, and a Literal Translation — fragments numbered 40 and 41, each footnoted 'Quoted by Hephaestion'
witnesses.edition: Project Gutenberg e-text #57390 (based on the London edition), pp. 96-97
witnesses.note: Modern public-domain reprint of the Hephaestion testimonium, kept as two separately numbered fragments (40, 41) with a note that fr. 41 'seems to be the beginning of a different ode.' Text as printed: 'Ἔρος δαὖτέ μ᾽ ὀ λυσιμελης δόνει, γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον.' / 'Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἔμεθεν μεν ἀπήχθετο φροντίσδην, ἐπὶ δ᾽ Ἀνδρομέδαν πότῃ.'

witnesses.source: Greek Wikisource, 'Επιγράμματα Σαπφούς' (page states its text is copied from Edmonds' Lyra Graeca vol. I [1922], reordered to follow Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci numbering) — 'Επίγραμμα 40' (marked as = Edmonds' own fr. 81)
witnesses.edition: el.wikisource.org, transcription of J. M. Edmonds, Lyra Graeca I (Loeb, 1922)
witnesses.note: Gives only the Eros couplet under this number: 'Ἔρος δαὖτέ μ᾽ ὀ λυσιμέλης δόνει / γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον,' agreeing with Wharton and with the Consbruch main text (δαὖτέ). The Ἄτθι couplet is not present as a separate transcription on this page.

witnesses.source: Greek Wikisource, 'Ύμνοι και Επιθαλάμια' (page header attributes its text to 'H. T. Wharton (1895), αποσπάσματα') — 'Απόσπασμα 40-41'
witnesses.edition: el.wikisource.org
witnesses.note: Gives both couplets together: 'Ἔρος δηὖτέ μ᾽ ὀ λυσιμέλης δόνει / γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον, / Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἔμεθεν μὲν ἀπήχθετο / φροντίσδην, ἐπὶ δ᾽ Ἀνδρομέδαν πότηι.' Note this reads δηὖτέ, which diverges from Wharton's actual printed text (δαὖτέ) as verified directly against the Gutenberg edition — likely a transcription inconsistency on this Wikisource page rather than a confirmed separate ancient variant; flagged, not resolved.

sourced.variants:
Numbering: the couplet 'Ἔρος δαῦτέ...ὄρπετον' = Sappho fr. 130 Voigt/Lobel-Page; the couplet 'Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽...πότη' = Sappho fr. 131 Voigt/Lobel-Page. Hephaestion's own citation numbers them 'Sapph. 40' and 'Sapph. 41' (a Bergk-derived numbering also followed by Wharton); Edmonds' Lyra Graeca instead numbers the pair as a single fragment, 81 ('πρὸς Ἄτθιδα'), reflecting how his source (Hephaestion) quotes them together as one continuous illustration of the acatalectic Aeolic tetrameter, even though editors judge them the openings of two different odes (so noted explicitly by Wharton).

No papyrus witness is known for this fragment; its entire ancient transmission is via the Hephaestion tradition (his Enchiridion plus the derivative Scholia B), not any papyrus.

Manuscript variants within the main Enchiridion witness (Consbruch's apparatus, p. 23, keyed to line numbers 19-22 of the printed page):
- line 19 (Ἔρος δαῦτέ μ᾽ ὁ λυσιμελὴς δόνει): codd. D, I read ἔρως (for ἔρος) and δονεῖ (for δόνει); text follows cod. A.
- line 20 (γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον): a variant "γλυκὺ πικρόν" (as two separate words, rather than the compound γλυκύπικρον) is registered in the apparatus (siglum unclear in the scanned copy).
- line 21 (Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἔμεθεν μὲν ἀπήχθετο): cod. A reads Ἄτθι σοι; codd. D, I read Ἄτθις σοι (nominative Ἄτθις rather than vocative Ἄτθι) and ἐμέθεν.
- line 22 (φροντίσδην, ἐπὶ δ᾽ Ἀνδρομέδαν πότη): the word printed as φροντίσδην is R. Bentley's conjecture; all manuscripts (codd.) actually transmit the unmetrical/corrupt φροντίς δ᾽ ἦν. Cod. A reads πότη; codd. D, I read πότε.

Manuscript variants within the second (Scholia B) witness (Consbruch's apparatus, p. 214-215, ms. classes Y = codd. p,k and Z = third scholia class):
- Ἄτθι: ms. class Y reads αὐτοῖς instead.
- φροντίσδην: ms. class Y again gives the corrupt φροντίς δ᾽ ἦν (matching the corruption in the main Enchiridion tradition), and ποτέ (for πότη).
- ms. class Z omits the Ἄτθι-couplet (both of its lines) entirely.

Orthographic/accentual differences among the modern print witnesses (not manuscript-attested, but visible across the fetched editions): δαῦτέ (Consbruch main text; Wharton; Edmonds-via-Wikisource) vs δηὖτέ (the Wikisource 'Ύμνοι' page, apparently inconsistent with its own stated Wharton source); πότη (Consbruch, cod. A) vs πότῃ (Wharton) vs πότηι (Wikisource 'Ύμνοι' page) — the last two are simply different modern conventions for writing the Aeolic dative ending, not substantive variants.
sourced.caveats:
All Greek text above was extracted from real fetched sources (archive.org OCR scan of Consbruch's 1906 Teubner edition of Hephaestion; Project Gutenberg's e-text of Wharton 1885; two Greek-Wikisource pages), not reconstructed from memory. One category of correction was made to the raw OCR of the archive.org Hephaestion scan: a handful of characters were plainly scanning artifacts rather than real textual variants (e.g. "uw" for μ᾽, a tripled-diacritic "ὄὕὄρπετον" for ὄρπετον, and "ἴκτϑι" for Ἄτθι — this last confirmed as OCR noise, not a variant, because the same source's own apparatus criticus at that point explicitly glosses the lemma as ἀτϑί/Ἄτθι, and the word appears correctly as Ἄτθι in the source's own second (Scholia B) quotation of the same line). These corrections were made only where the source's own apparatus or its own duplicate quotation confirmed the intended reading — no wording was supplied from outside knowledge.

The apparatus-criticus siglum for the 'γλυκὺ πικρόν' (two-word) variant on line 20 could not be read with confidence from the scan (rendered only as an ambiguous "4Ρ)" in the OCR); I have reported that a variant exists there without asserting which witness carries it.

The discrepancy between the two Wikisource pages over δηὖτέ vs δαὖτέ (see variants) is reported as found, but I was not able to independently verify which, if either, reflects a genuine manuscript-level variant versus a modern transcription slip on Wikisource, since Wharton's own text (checked directly against Gutenberg) and Edmonds' text (checked directly against both the archive.org OCR scan of Lyra Graeca and the Wikisource transcription sourced to it) both agree on δαὖτέ, leaving the 'Ύμνοι' Wikisource page's δηὖτέ unconfirmed elsewhere among the sources fetched for this task.

Per the task's absolute rule, no English (or other modern-language) translation or paraphrase of Sappho's actual wording appears anywhere above; all English text is confined to bibliographic/philological description of sourcing and manuscript variants.
sourced.note: Definition of Eros as bittersweet and limb-loosening; address to Atthis.

sourced.id: Sappho fr. 132 (Voigt / Lobel-Page numbering; "on Cleis, likened to a golden flower")
sourced.greek_text:
Ἔστι μοι κάλα πάϊς, χρυσίοισιν ἀνθέμοισιν
ἐμφέρην ἔχοισα μόρφαν, Κλῆϊσ' ἀγαπάτα,
ἀντί τᾶς ἔγω οὐδὲ Λυδίαν παῖσαν οὐδ' ἔρανναν.

witnesses.source: Hephaestion, Ἐγχειρίδιον περὶ μέτρου (Enchiridion / Handbook of Metre) — chapter on ἀσυνάρτητα ("unconnectable") verse-forms, where the two lines are cited and metrically scanned as an example of a trochaic dimeter acatalectic + an iambic of three-and-a-half feet (with a variant scansion, procatalectic + acatalectic dimeter, for line 1)
witnesses.edition: Text as printed by Henry Thornton Wharton, 'Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings, and a Literal Translation,' 3rd ed. (London: John Lane, 1895), fragment numbered '85' in Wharton's own sequence (his text follows Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci)
witnesses.url: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/57390/57390-h/57390-h.htm (Project Gutenberg eBook #57390; fetched directly — Greek given as proper Unicode with accents, not OCR)
witnesses.note: Primary source used for the Greek text quoted above, extracted verbatim from the HTML (lines/paragraphs corresponding to fragment '85'). A page-scan copy of the same edition is also at archive.org, identifier sapphomemoirtext00sappiala, but its OCR text (…_djvu.txt) renders the Greek font as unreadable Latin-lookalike garbage and was not used as a source of readings, only as confirmation the same fragment/citation is present.

witnesses.source: Same ancient witness (Hephaestion, Handbook of Metre, chapter on 'unconnectable' metres), independently re-set in a second early-20th-century public-domain edition
witnesses.edition: J. M. Edmonds, 'Lyra Graeca,' vol. I (Loeb Classical Library, London/New York, 1922), fragment numbered '130' ('To Cleis') in Edmonds' own sequence — NOT the same as his fragment '132', which is an unrelated Sappho fragment (Etymologicum Magnum, on ὀφθαλμοῖσιν)
witnesses.note: OCR of the Greek in this scan is badly corrupted (e.g. the first line appears as '£cev: uo: kdAa ais' and 'xpvaíowiv àv0éuoiwiw' for what is legible as Ἔστι μοι κάλα πάις / χρυσίοισιν ἀνθέμοισιν, and 'àvri ràs éyc ov8€ ... Avbí/av ... Gea» ov8? épivvav' for ἀντὶ τᾶς ἔγω οὐδὲ ... Λυδίαν ... παῖσαν οὐδ' ἔρανναν). It is corroborative only — confirms wording and the identical Hephaestion attribution — and was NOT used to establish the quoted Greek text itself, because the OCR cannot be trusted letter-for-letter. Edmonds' apparatus note (also OCR-degraded) preserves a genuine ancient variant: 'Sch. Heph.[aestionem]: the ancient metrists made Κλ[έϊς] ⏑–⏑ ... edd. who suppose them wrong read ... taking [χρυσ. as 3 syllables and] Κλέϊς and Λυδ. as 2 [syllables]' — i.e. the scholia vetera on Hephaestion record an ancient/medieval dispute over how many syllables the name Κλέϊς and the adjective χρυσίοισιν count for metrically.

sourced.variants: All witnesses located trace to a single ultimate ancient source — Hephaestion's metrical handbook (Ἐγχειρίδιον περὶ μέτρου), as read and discussed by the ancient/Byzantine scholia on Hephaestion (Σχόλια εἰς Ἡφαιστίωνα). No papyrus witness and no second independent quoting author (e.g. Athenaeus, Strabo, Dionysius of Halicarnassus) was found for this fragment. Differences observed between the two public-domain print editions consulted are editorial/orthographic, not independent manuscript traditions: (1) Wharton/Bergk-based text prints the girl's name as Κλῆϊσ' (spelled with η, elided before the following vowel of ἀγαπάτα) — the scholia on Hephaestion, as excerpted in Edmonds' apparatus, show that ancient metrists and later editors disagreed on whether this name/word scans as two or three syllables, which correlates with the η/ε spelling difference (Κλῆϊς vs. the commoner Κλέϊς) found across editions of Sappho. (2) The Wharton/Bergk text accents the preposition as ἀντί (acute) rather than the grave ἀντὶ that ordinary Greek accentuation rules would call for before a following word — likely a 19th-century typesetting/editorial choice rather than a manuscript variant. (3) ἔρανναν is accented on the first syllable in this text; other printings of the same word (an Aeolic form of "lovely") sometimes appear as ἐράνναν. These are the only textual differences that could be verified from the fetched sources; no substantive wording variants (i.e., different words) between witnesses were found.
sourced.caveats: (1) This fragment (Sappho fr. 132 in the now-standard Lobel-Page/Voigt numbering used in the task) is numbered differently in each historical edition consulted: fr. '85' in Wharton (1895, following Bergk), fr. '130' in Edmonds' Loeb Lyra Graeca (1922). Readers should not confuse Edmonds' own fragment '132' (a different, unrelated Sappho fragment from the Etymologicum Magnum) with Voigt's fr. 132 discussed here. (2) I was not able to fetch the modern standard critical edition (Lobel–Page 1955 or Voigt 1971), which is not in the public domain and was not found openly hosted; the Greek text given above is therefore drawn from 19th/early-20th-century public-domain editions (ultimately based on Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci) rather than the current standard apparatus criticus, and may differ from Voigt's text in minor accentuation/orthography (see 'variants' above) even though the wording is identical. (3) I attempted to consult Bergk's own Poetae Lyrici Graeci, vol. III (4th ed., 1882; archive.org id poetaelyricigrae03berguoft) directly, but its Greek-font OCR was too corrupted to locate or quote the fragment reliably within the time/tooling available, so it is not cited as a source of readings, only mentioned as the basis both Wharton and (indirectly) later editions used. (4) A search for a papyrus witness (P.Oxy., P.Sapph.Obbink, Berlin papyri, etc.) for this specific fragment turned up nothing; the balance of evidence from the sources fetched here is that fr. 132 survives solely through the medieval manuscript transmission of Hephaestion's handbook and its scholia, not through any papyrus find. (5) Per the task's hard rule, no English (or other modern-language) rendering of Sappho's Greek appearing on any fetched page has been included, quoted, or paraphrased anywhere above — only the Greek text and bibliographic/metrical citation material.
sourced.note: Short poem on her daughter Cleis, likened to a golden flower.

sourced.greek_text:
Δέδυκε μὲν ἀ σελάννα
καὶ Πληΐαδες, μέσαι δέ
νύκτες, πάρα δ' ἔρχετ' ὤρα,
ἔγω δὲ μόνα κατεύδω.

witnesses.source: Hephaestion, Enchiridion (Ἐγχειρίδιον περὶ μέτρων), section on the Ionicum a maiore / Ionic-trochaic mixed cola (the 'hagesichorean'); quoted anonymously, with no author named, as a bare metrical example. This is the SOLE ancient testimonium for the fragment - no papyrus witness (P.Oxy., P.Sapph.Obbink, P.GC. inv. 105, Berlin papyri, etc.) preserves any part of it.
witnesses.edition: Text as printed by Theodor Bergk, Poetae Lyrici Graeci, vol. 3 (Sappho et reliqui melici), 4th ed. (Leipzig: Teubner, repr. 1882), Sappho fr. 52 [= fr. 54 in Bergk's earlier numbering], p. 107, citing 'Hephaest. 65'; critical apparatus/commentary on the same fragment appears a few pages later (ad Fr. 52).
witnesses.note: Fetched as OCR'd plain text (archive.org identifier poetaelyricigrae03berguoft). Bergk's own apparatus (in Latin, ad loc.) states he restored the four-line colometry against Hephaestion's manuscript tradition, which presents the citation as two long lines: 'Eadem Apostol. V 98. C. Gaisford binos versiculos coniunxit, quae discriptio non probanda. Sapphoni tribuit haec Stephanus.' I.e.: Gaisford's edition of Hephaestion joined the quotation into two verses (the manuscript arrangement); Bergk rejects that colometry and restores four lines; Bergk further notes that it was the Renaissance editor Stephanus (Henri Estienne), not Hephaestion, who first assigned the fragment to Sappho by name.

witnesses.source: Same Hephaestion passage, independently re-set from the manuscript/editorial tradition of Hephaestion (Consbruch-type page/section numbering 'Heph. 70').

sourced.variants:
All variation attaches to a single ultimate source (Hephaestion's Enchiridion); there is no papyrus vs. quoting-author split for this fragment, only manuscript/editorial variation within the Hephaestion tradition, consistently reported across the fetched witnesses:

1) Line 1, the moon-word: σελάννα (double -ν-: so Bergk PLG³ fr.52, Edmonds Loeb fr.111, Wharton fr.52, and Voigt 1971 as quoted on Wikipedia) vs. σελάνα (single -ν-: Denys Page, PMG adesp. 976, per Wikipedia's citation of Page 1962 p.520). Bergk's own apparatus (fetched, ad Fr.52, 'V.1') explicitly records manuscript disagreement between σελάννα and σελάνα among Hephaestion's codices, and floats a third possible Aeolic spelling; he prints σελάννα as his own restoration.

2) Line 3, the verb of 'passing': ἔρχετ' (unaspirated/psilotic form: Bergk, Edmonds, Wharton, Voigt) vs. ἔρχεθ' (aspirated form: the reading Bergk says stood in the manuscripts before his emendation - 'V.3 ἔρχετ᾽ ... scripsi, legebatur ἔρχεθ᾽' - and the reading Page prints in PMG, per Wikipedia).

3) Line 4, 'I sleep': κατεύδω (unaspirated/psilotic: Bergk, Edmonds, Wharton, Voigt) vs. καθεύδω (aspirated, the manuscript paradosis per the same Bergk apparatus note: '...et v.4 κατεύδω ... scripsi, legebatur ... καθεύδω'). This third variant is not mentioned by the Wikipedia summary of Page's differences but is explicitly attested in Bergk's own fetched critical apparatus.

Together, (1)-(3) form a single coherent editorial fault-line: the psilotic/Aeolic-looking forms (σελάννα, ἔρχετ', κατεύδω) are Bergk's 19th-century emendations meant to make the fragment's dialect consistent with Sappho's Lesbian/Aeolic vernacular (psilosis = loss of aspiration), while the aspirated forms (σελάνα or σελάννα with single-ν, ἔρχεθ', καθεύδω) are closer to what Hephaestion's manuscripts actually transmit. Editors who accept Sapphic authorship (Voigt, Campbell, Edmonds, Rayor & Lardinois, Neri) print the emended/Aeolicized text; Page, who classifies the poem as anonymous (adespoton), keeps the manuscripts' non-Aeolic forms, which is itself part of his argument against Sapphic authorship.

4) Colometry/line-division: Hephaestion's manuscripts present the quotation as TWO long lines (each pairing two metrical cola), not four; Gaisford's edition of Hephaestion preserved this two-line division ('Gaisford binos versiculos coniunxit'). The now-standard FOUR-line arrangement (used in every modern edition, including the one given above) is an editorial restoration first made by Bergk himself ('quae discriptio non probanda' = Bergk judges Gaisford's two-line division wrong), a fact independently confirmed by the Wikipedia article's footnote citing Clay 1970 n.1: 'Hephaestion arranges the poem over two lines; the four-line arrangement was first restored by Theodor Bergk.'

5) Attribution: Hephaestion's own text carries no author's name for these verses - it is quoted purely as an anonymous metrical specimen. Bergk's apparatus notes 'Sapphoni tribuit haec Stephanus' (it was the Renaissance scholar Stephanus/Henri Estienne who first ascribed it to Sappho), while the Wikipedia article instead credits the Renaissance grammarian Arsenius Apostolius with the first ascription to Sappho. Either way, all fetched sources agree Sappho's name is a post-antique editorial addition, not part of the Hephaestion witness itself - hence Page's classification as PMG fr. adesp. 976 (fragmenta adespota, 'of unknown authorship') alongside Voigt's inclusion of the same text as Sappho fr. 168B.
sourced.caveats:
- No papyrus witness exists for this fragment. Unlike many other Sappho fragments (e.g. P.Oxy. 1231, P.Oxy. 7, P.Sapph.Obbink, P.GC. inv. 105, the Berlin papyrus), 168B/adesp. 976 survives ONLY through the indirect quotation chain rooted in Hephaestion's 2nd-century-CE metrical handbook, itself known only through medieval manuscript copies (an abridged/epitomized version of the original Enchiridion, per the Wikipedia summary of Clay 2011).
- Because the poem is quoted purely as a metrical illustration, Hephaestion preserves only these four cola; no larger context or surrounding stanzas survive, and most scholars (per the fetched Wikipedia summary) believe the transmitted text is only a fragment of a longer original (though Diskin Clay has argued it is complete as it stands).
- Authorship is genuinely disputed among editors, not just a matter of numbering: Eva-Maria Voigt (1971), David Campbell (1982), Camillo Neri (2021), and Diane Rayor & André Lardinois (2014) include it in Sappho's corpus (hence 'Sappho fr. 168B Voigt'); Denys Page, Edgar Lobel, and Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff treated it as anonymous (hence 'PMG fr. adesp. 976'). This dispute is reflected directly in the primary editions I fetched: Edmonds (1922) and Wharton (1887) print it among Sappho's fragments without flagging doubt in the Greek-text apparatus itself, while Bergk's apparatus records the post-antique (Renaissance) origin of the Sappho attribution, and Page's textual choices (σελάνα, ἔρχεθ') track with his anonymous classification.
- I was NOT able to fetch Eva-Maria Voigt's Sappho et Alcaeus (1971) or Denys Page's Poetae Melici Graecae (1962) directly online - these 20th-century critical editions are not freely available as open full text within the tools available this session. Their specific readings are reported here only via a direct, cited quotation embedded in the English Wikipedia article 'Midnight poem', which I did fetch directly and which explicitly gives page citations (Voigt 1971, pp. 147-8; Page 1962, p. 520) for the Greek forms it quotes. This is a secondary-source relay for those two specific citations, though the underlying Greek wording is independently corroborated by the three primary 19th/20th-century editions (Bergk, Wharton, Edmonds) I fetched and cross-checked directly.
- The Bergk (1882) and Wharton (1887/1907) texts were recovered from archive.org OCR (djvu.txt) of 19th-century Greek typefaces. The OCR engine transliterates polytonic Greek inconsistently (sometimes rendering the same letter differently within one paragraph, and using different substitution schemes on different pages/scans), so individual characters in the raw fetched text are visually garbled (e.g. 'Aé8vke uév à aéXavva', 'Ae6uK€ juev a ceAavva', 'Zdüvxe ubv d GsAdvva' - three different OCR renderings of the identical printed Greek line 'Δέδυκε μὲν ἀ σελάννα'). I decoded these against one another and against the cleanly-encoded Wikipedia/Voigt quotation to arrive at the verbatim Greek text given above with high confidence, since all three independently-scanned primary editions agree letter-for-letter once decoded. The Latin critical-apparatus prose surrounding the verses (Bergk's notes on manuscript sigla 'A' vs. 'ceteri') is reported in the variants field as a confident paraphrase of that apparatus rather than a claimed perfect verbatim transcription, given the same OCR noise.
- Per the task's absolute rule, no English (or other modern-language) translation of the poem's words has been included anywhere above; all English text quoted is either bibliographic/citation material or Wikipedia's own encyclopedic description of the scholarly debate (not a rendering of Sappho's/the fragment's wording), and the Latin critical-apparatus prose from Bergk is scholarly commentary, not a translation of the Greek verses themselves.

Two independent fetched transcriptions of the P.Sapph.Obbink text were compared line-by-line (digitalsappho.org vs. CHS Classical Inquiries/Nagy) and are identical in wording except for:

(1) SUBSTANTIVE VARIANT — line 17 in digitalsappho.org's numbering (= line 21 in the CHS/papyrus-column numbering), in the clause about Larichos "lifting his/the head":
  - digitalsappho.org (citing Obbink 2014, ZPE 189:49): "κἄμμες, αἴ κε τὰν κεφάλα̣ν ἀέρρ̣η" (τὰν = the article/demonstrative, fem. acc. sg., "the head")
  - CHS Classical Inquiries (Nagy, both 2015 essays, "as edited by Dirk Obbink"): "κ̣ἄμμεϲ, αἴ κε ϝὰν κεφάλα̣ν ἀέρρ̣η" (ϝὰν = digamma-initial possessive/reflexive form, "his own head")

(2) ORTHOGRAPHIC/TYPOGRAPHIC ONLY (not substantive): digitalsappho.org uses standard sigma (σ/ς); CHS/Nagy uses lunate sigma (ϲ) throughout, per papyrological house style. Minor accentuation differences also occur (e.g. "τὰ μὲν̣" vs "τὰ μέν̣"; "Λάρι̣χος" vs "Λάρι̣χοϲ") that are conventions of transcription, not competing readings.

No variant apparatus for P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 5 could be obtained (see caveats) — so it is not possible to report whether/how that second papyrus's readings diverge from P.Sapph.Obbink at any point of overlap.

sourced.variants:
The two ancient papyrus witnesses are not independent poems but overlapping copies/portions of the same text, and P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16 for the most part CONFIRMS rather than contradicts P. Sapph. Obbink; the "variants" are mainly (a) places where one papyrus preserves letters the other does not, and (b) a couple of genuine cruces of interpretation:

- Line 1 (Kypris-Poem numbering): P. Sapph. Obbink gives θαμε ̣ ̣ (articulated θαμέωϲ by Obbink); P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16.1 independently gives ]θαμε ̣[, which earlier editors (working from P. Oxy. 1231 alone) read as θαμέω[ν (Hunt) or θαμέω[ϲ (Diehl¹) — i.e. the new papyrus is used by Obbink to help decide between these earlier competing supplements to the *old* fragment.
- Line 2: P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16.2 gives ]τ'τινα[, read by Hunt as ὄ]ττινα[ϲ γὰρ — a different case-ending/continuation than Obbink's ὄττινα δὴ φιλείη from the new papyrus; the new papyrus's ὄττινα (accusative singular, not plural ὄττινας) is preferred by Obbink, effectively overriding Hunt's old restoration.
- Line 3: P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16.3 gives ]λιϲταπα[; Obbink notes this rules out an earlier proposed identification of these lines with a quotation in Etymologicum Magnum 449.34, because that quotation lacks the letters πα found here in both papyri.
- Line 4: P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16.4 has NO letters at this point ("nothing here but blank papyrus"), because its column was laid out with a shorter adonean line at this position — i.e. an apparent structural/layout difference between the two copies at this line, not a wording variant.
- Line 6: P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16.6 gives ]·γονωμ[ with a raised punctuation point that Obbink says may "counterindicate" reading the sequence as continuous ...αντιγονω..., i.e. the older papyrus's punctuation is used as evidence AGAINST one candidate reading of the newer papyrus.
- Lines 7 and 9: P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16.7 (]αι μ'ουπρ[) and fr. 16.9 (]αι, blank; and separately ]ϲέ·θελω[) are used by Obbink to confirm and extend the new papyrus's traces (]μ' οὐ πρ- and ]ϲέ, θέλω[ respectively).
- Lines 10–15 (old Voigt numbering)/30–33 (Obbink's continuous numbering): only P. Oxy. 1231 preserves letters at all here (the new papyrus is lost/illegible past line 29/9); within that stretch, lines 11–12 are not securely read from either papyrus but are supplied instead from the quotation in Apollonius Dyscolus, De Pronominibus — i.e. for those two lines the wording rests on a testimonium rather than on either papyrus.

Overall Obbink's stated conclusion (quoted verbatim from the article) is that the new papyrus "substantially augments Sappho fr. 26 Voigt (as previously known from P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16), previous reconstructions of which it corrects as it invites new ones" — i.e. the "variant" at the level of the whole fragment is really a revision of prior scholarly reconstruction (Hunt's, Diehl's) rather than a disagreement between the two papyri themselves, which the editor treats as copies of the same underlying text.
sourced.caveats:
1. WebSearch was unavailable for this session (budget exhausted before I could run any query), so all sourcing here comes from direct WebFetch/curl retrieval of specific URLs rather than search discovery; I located the URLs by following links inside pages I could fetch (Wikipedia's "Brothers Poem" external link -> digitalsappho.org -> the PDF link on that site's own citation for fr. 26 -> Obbink's original ZPE 189 (2014) article PDF). I verified the digitalsappho.org page's Greek text by fetching the raw HTML directly via curl (not just the WebFetch summarizer) to rule out transcription drift from the fetch tool's intermediate model; I then located and read the primary publication (Obbink's ZPE article PDF) directly with a Python PDF-text extraction, which is the authoritative source used for greek_text above.

2. I was NOT able to independently fetch the original 1914 Grenfell–Hunt edition of P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16 (the pre-2014-known witness, = old Sappho fr. 26 Voigt) as a standalone source in this session — archive.org's copy of "The Oxyrhynchus Papyri Part X" appears to be a lending-library scan without accessible open full text via the API calls I made. All P. Oxy. 1231 fr. 16 readings given above are therefore secondhand, as quoted inside Obbink 2014's apparatus criticus (itself a legitimate, citable primary papyrological publication), not independently checked against the 1914 edition itself.

3. Likewise I did NOT independently fetch Apollonius Dyscolus, De Pronominibus (Schneider's edition) for lines 11–12; that couplet is reported here strictly as Obbink cites it (crediting Voigt's apparatus on Sa. 26.11–12). Treat Witness C as unverified secondhand until an independent look at Apollonius Dyscolus's text is done.

4. The fragment is extremely lacunose (large papyrus damage); most "words" in the diplomatic and even the articulated text are partial, bracketed, or marked with underdots by the editor to indicate uncertain letters — this is preserved as-is in the Greek text above, exactly as printed in the source, not smoothed over.

5. Per the task's absolute rule, no English (or other modern-language) translation of any of this material appears anywhere in this output; the fetched pages (both digitalsappho.org and the Obbink PDF) do contain English translations and extensive English commentary alongside the Greek, which I read but deliberately excluded in full from every field above.

6. Note on sigma glyphs: the Obbink ZPE article (a papyrological edition) prints the papyrological lunate sigma "ϲ" throughout; digitalsappho.org's teaching transcription instead prints standard modern Greek σ/ς. This is a typographic/editorial convention difference between the two renderings of the same composite text, not a genuine textual variant, and I have kept Obbink's own lunate-sigma printing in the "articulated text" and "P. Oxy. 1231" sections above since that is the actual verbatim primary edition.
sourced.note: Newly recovered continuation/correction of fr. 26 Voigt from the same 2014 papyrus, addressing Kypris/Aphrodite on recurring erotic suffering; substantially revises the sense of the previously known fragmentary lines.
